hypothesis.hypothesis:
Cycle count stays exactly the same; all gain is Fmax. Each cut removes
at least one LUT level or a >1.5 ns fanout net from one family.

A. Regfile written from the MEM stage; no write-first bypass (F3).
   reg_file.sv loses the `w_en && w_addr == rs_addr` bypass: the read is
   plain LUT-RAM plus the x0 zero term. Top-level wiring drives the
   regfile write port from the EX/MEM occupant instead of MEM/WB:
   w_addr = EX/MEM.rd, w_data = mem_stage's fwd_val (load data or ALU
   result, the value ID already forwards), w_en = EX/MEM.fwd_ok
   (a flop: reg_write && rd != 0 && !misaligned-jump &&
   !misaligned-mem, cleared on bubbles). Correctness: an instruction in
   MEM is covered in ID by the existing fwd_mem mux in the same cycle it
   writes, and it is in the RAM from the next cycle, so the MEM/WB
   occupant needs no bypass. During a dmem stall the held LOAD writes
   garbage load data each cycle. That is harmless: ID/EX is frozen
   (stall_id and no flush during dmem stall), so nothing captures a
   regfile read of that rd until the completing cycle, which rewrites
   the correct value, and ID forwards it via fwd_mem in that same cycle.
   So w_en needs no dmem_ready term. Keep the RVFI rd_wdata path
   unchanged. wb_stage still forms w_data from MEM/WB for RVFI only
   (pruned in the timed netlist). The forward_unit / id_stage comments
   change: I-3 is now covered by the regfile itself. Drop the reg_file
   reset loop in favour of an `initial` zero fill, so Gowin maps a pure
   RAM16SDP array with no reset-emulation gating. Keep the x0 term as
   the last-level mux input, so formal still sees x0 == 0.

B. Two-level result OR (alu.sv, id_stage.sv, core_pkg.sv) (F2, F4).
   - ADD/SUB merge into one class RS_ADDSUB with a registered is_sub:
     addsub = a + (b ^ {32{is_sub}}) + is_sub (Gowin ALU ADDSUB mode,
     no extra LUT; one chain instead of two).
   - AND/OR/XOR merge into one pre-masked logic term driven by a
     registered 2-bit lop (00 none, 01 AND, 10 OR, 11 XOR), one LUT4
     {a_i, b_i, lop} per bit that is already 0 when not a logic op.
   - Flop-sourced classes are pre-combined early:
     (* syn_keep *) early_or = (sel_div & quo_q) | (sel_pre & pre).
   - Late fast_or = addsub&s | logic | sll&s | sr&s | early_or,
     i.e. five late inputs -> 2 LUT4 levels instead of 4.
   - SLT/SLTU (bit 0 only) join in the final `out` LUT together with
     fast_or[0] and mul_or[0], not at the bottom of bit 0's tree. SLT
     and SLTU share one 33-bit signed-selectable less-than
     ({a[31]&~uns, a} < {b[31]&~uns, b}, registered slt_uns bit), like
     the branch comparator, so there is one carry chain instead of two.
   Keep the syn_keep fast_or / mul_or late-join split from r4s0.

C. Branch equality without the bypass LUT (ex_stage.sv) (F5).
   The EX bypass selects are registered, so compute three flop-sourced
   equalities in parallel:
     eq_vv = (in.rs1_val == in.rs2_val), eq_rv = (res_q == in.rs2_val),
     eq_vr = (in.rs1_val == res_q)
   and select br_eq = fwd1 ? (fwd2 ? 1 : eq_rv) : (fwd2 ? eq_vr : eq_vv)
   in one LUT from registered bits. This removes the bypass LUT and its
   fanout-19 net from the eq tree. The less-than chain keeps the
   bypassed operands (the carry chain is fast). Also keep the
   redirect_e duplicate (syn_keep) as the only driver of the pc_w CE term.

D. Consumer-local copies of the EX/MEM result (ex_stage.sv) (F1, F2, F4).
   Add (* syn_keep = 1 *) duplicate flops of EX/MEM.alu_result, all
   loaded identically under the same stall enable: res_m_q feeds a
   dedicated DSP-only operand bypass (mul_a / mul_b muxes with their own
   syn_keep registered select copies), res_a_q feeds the ALU-A/AGU/lt
   muxes and res_b_q feeds alu_b. The original reg_q.alu_result keeps
   MEM (fwd_val, MEM/WB) and the eq compares. Each copy drives about 32
   loads instead of 70-110, so the placer can put it next to its
   consumer, which shortens the 1.2-3.0 ns first nets that start every
   family.

Estimate: each family loses ~1.0-1.5 ns of its ~10.1 ns, so
~9.0 ns -> ~110-114 MHz median, about +8-10% at unchanged cycles.
Risks: the DIV/ALTOPS handshake and mul_or late join are untouched.
The MEM-stage write changes regfile write timing, so the cocotb
forwarding tests and cosim (load-use under dmem stall) are the guards.
The RAM write data now depends on dmem DO -> load extract -> fwd_val,
one mux shorter than the existing dmem DO -> op_b path (9.94 ns), so it
should not become the new worst path.

Drive the regfile write port from the EX/MEM occupant: w_en = ex_mem_w.fwd_ok, w_addr = ex_mem_w.rd, w_data = mem_fwd_val. wb_stage output now only feeds RVFI rd_wdata (unchanged RVFI semantics).

lesson: - 2026-09-30 hyp-20260930-001-r5s0 (regression, -8.14%): Bundling five cuts for r4s0's tied ~10.1 ns families (MEM-stage regfile write with no write-first compare, a 2-level result OR with merged `is_sub ? a-b : a+b` and a pre-masked lop logic LUT, three parallel flop-sourced branch equalities, and syn_keep consumer-local copies of the EX/MEM result) dropped the place-option-0 Fmax from 98.7 to 88.2 MHz at unchanged cycles, because the new worst path (16.6 ns: registered DSP-bypass select -> DSP -> mul_or -> out[0]) went through a new level added after the multiplier when SLT was moved into the final `out` LUT, which undid r4s0's rule that only fast_or | mul_or may follow the DSP, and the merged add/sub then became a 26-cell `is_sub` path that probably did not map to one Gowin ADDSUB chain, while `(* syn_keep *)` on the enable-loaded duplicate flops put a CE-emulation LUT in front of D (dropping it for syn_preserve saved 114 LUTs but only 0.9 MHz); so fold any new term into fast_or rather than into the join after the late DSP product, confirm that a merged add/sub still maps to a single carry chain, and, because one bad cut hides the gain of the others, time each cut of a multi-family fix separately before combining them.

title: Decoupled front end: 2-entry bypassable fetch queue that keeps fetching through backend stalls, so imem stalls overlap load-use / dmem / div stalls
motivation:
The imem bus is not ready on ~22% of cycles. The xorshift sequence in
fpga/bench_stall_gen.sv (and in cosim) runs whether or not the core
asks for anything, and each cycle is an independent 100/128 accept.
Today the front end is lock-stepped to the back end. stall_if holds
the PC on every load-use, dmem and div stall, so the instruction
that was ready during a back-end stall is thrown away and fetched
again. That refetch then misses the bus 22% of the time. So imem
stall bubbles never overlap back-end stall cycles.
Rough CPI budget for the champion (r4s0: 4.49 M cycles for 10
iterations, CPI about 1.5-1.6):
  imem-not-ready bubbles  ~0.28-0.31 per instruction, the largest
                          single loss (~20% of cycles)
  taken-redirect bubble   ~0.12
  dmem stalls             ~0.08
  load-use                ~0.06-0.10
imem stalls are the largest loss that nothing so far has attacked.
Every earlier round went after Fmax or branch bubbles.
Also, the champion's PC enable is fed by stall_if =
load_use(raw imem rs1/rs2 vs ID/EX.rd) | !imem_ready | dmem_stall |
div_stall. A decoupled front end removes that compare chain from the
PC CE, since the PC no longer waits on the back end.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Split fetch from decode with a small instruction queue (IQ) that can
be bypassed, so the front end fetches whenever the bus is ready and
the queue has room, not only when the back end advances.

Front end (if_stage.sv):
  - Add a 2-entry IQ (pc[31:2] + instr + valid per entry) as a shift
    register, with a registered occupancy count occ (0..2) and
    registered one-hot valid bits.
  - PC enable = redirect_ce | (imem_ready & (occ != 2)). Every term is
    a flop or the existing kept redirect copy. load-use, dmem_stall
    and div_stall no longer reach the PC. The PC D-mux is unchanged
    (redirect ? target : pc + 1).
  - ID input: if occ != 0 (registered select) it is the IQ head,
    otherwise the raw imem word with pc_w. valid_id = q_valid0 |
    imem_ready, both flops.
  - consume = !stall_id (ID/EX loads this cycle).
    push = imem_ready & (occ != 2) & !redirect & !(occ == 0 & consume),
    pop = consume & (occ != 0).
    On push the word goes to entry occ - pop. On pop the shift is
    q0 <= q1 (or the word just fetched).
  - On redirect, clear the IQ valid bits and occ, and drop the fetch
    of that cycle (it is wrong-path). This gives the same 1-bubble
    redirect penalty as today.
Hazard unit: load-use compares the ID-input instruction (mux output)
against ID/EX.rd, not raw io_imemData. stall_if is deleted.
flush_id = (redirect | load_use | !valid_id) & !dmem_stall &
!div_stall. stall_id is unchanged. The instruction held by a
load-use, dmem or div stall stays at the IQ head, or is pushed there
if it came in on the bypass path, so it is presented again next cycle
without refetching.
Forwarding is still exact. ID/EX, EX/MEM and MEM/WB keep moving in
lockstep (stall_id still covers every dmem and div stall). Only the
PC and the IQ move independently, and they hold no architectural
state that forwarding reads.

Cycle effect: each back-end stall cycle (dmem, load-use, div) now
lets the front end bank one instruction with probability 0.78. Each
banked instruction later hides one imem-not-ready cycle, unless a
taken redirect flushes it first (P(used) is about 0.6, from 8-9
instructions between taken redirects and a 22% per-cycle stall
rate). A hand estimate from that gave 5-6% fewer cycles, but a
trace-driven model disagrees. The model uses 600K timed-region CoreMark
instructions from test/cosim/reference.py, the exact xorshift
imem/dmem ready sequence, load-use on the raw rs1/rs2 fields, dmem
freezes, the 35-cycle DIV, and a 1-bubble taken redirect. Its
baseline CPI is 1.517, and it measures:
  depth 1: -0.2%   depth 2: +1.5%   depth 3: +1.7% fewer cycles.
Back-end stalls are too rare for the front end to get far ahead, and
taken redirects flush the queue first. Depth 1 loses because a
full 1-entry queue blocks the fetch in the cycle it drains. So the
honest cycle gain is ~1.5% at depth 2. That only pays if the PC-CE
simplification (no load-use compare on pc_w CE) gains Fmax, or if
the design is later combined with a predictor (r4s2's BTB): then
redirects stop flushing the queue and banked entries live longer.

Fmax: the worst path stays the EX loop alu_result -> ALU ->
alu_result, which this change does not touch. The PC-CE family loses
its load-use compare (a small gain). The new cost is one registered-
select 2:1 mux level on the ID-input word and pc (imem -> decode /
imm / regfile address / load-use -> ID/EX). This path starts at flops
(the LFSR imem word, the IQ head) and ends at ID/EX. The implementer
must check with `make timing` that it stays below the EX loop. If it
is close, duplicate the IQ-head select flop (syn_keep) so the
rs1/rs2 regfile-address copy and the decode copy do not share one
high-fanout net.

lesson: - 2026-09-30 hyp-20260930-002-r5s1 (regression, +1.72%): A decoupled front end (2-entry bypassable IQ, PC CE = redirect_ce | imem_ready & occ!=2, load-use compared on the IQ-head/raw-imem mux output, stall_if deleted) scored 236.94 vs r4s0's 232.94, which fits the trace-driven model's ~1.5% cycle cut at an unchanged ~104.7 MHz implied Fmax and not the 5-6% hand estimate, because back-end stalls (load-use, dmem, DIV) are too rare for fetch to bank many words ahead and each taken redirect flushes the queue before a banked word can hide an imem-not-ready cycle; taking the load-use compare off the PC CE also gained no Fmax because the EX alu_result loop sets the clock, so for stall-overlap ideas trust the exact-xorshift trace model over hand estimates, and revisit the IQ only on top of a BTB (r4s2), where predicted-taken branches stop flushing it.

title: Registered look-ahead BTB on r4s0: lookup the next fetch PC one cycle early, flop the prediction, verify in EX with a pt-flipped inv bit
motivation:
In the r4s0 champion (104.6 MHz, 4,491,817 cycles), IF and ID share a
cycle and EX redirects, so every taken branch or JAL costs one bubble.
The ISS trace in r1s2 counts 12.2% of retired instructions as taken
transfers. r4s2's 32-entry PC-indexed LUT-RAM BTB, built on r3s1, is the
only predictor here that kept its IPC gain: cycles fell from 4.49M to
4.20M (-6.44%) and Fmax did not drop (90.7 vs 89.4 MHz). It lost only to
r4s0's orthogonal EX cuts.

Porting r4s2 as-is onto r4s0 is risky, because its fetch path is
combinational within one cycle:
  PC flop -> LUT-RAM async read -> 8-bit tag compare -> pt -> 30-bit PC
  mux -> redirect mux -> PC
That is about 6-7 LUT/RAM levels plus a 30-bit fan-out. It fit r3s1's
11.2 ns period, but r4s0's is 9.56 ns and r4s0's worst path is only
5 cells. LESSONS says to re-time this path against r4s0 before counting
on the IPC. At a 4.6% acceptance bar and a ~6.4% cycle cut, the port can
lose at most ~2% Fmax. So the predictor must add no combinational depth
to the PC loop and none to EX->redirect->PC.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Build the BTB as a look-ahead predictor with a registered output. The
lookup for the PC that will be fetched next cycle runs during the
current cycle and ends in a flop. The PC mux then selects on a flop.

1. rtl/btb.sv (new): 32 entries, direct-mapped, distributed LUT-RAM
   (syn_ramstyle "distributed_ram"). One async read port and one sync
   write port. Index a[6:2], 8-bit partial tag a[14:7], target [19:2]
   (18 bits), 2-bit counter: 28 bits, 14 RAM16 blocks, as in r4s2. There
   are no valid bits and no reset, because EX verifies every prediction.
   Add an `initial` zero fill for Verilator only.

2. IF (if_stage.sv): add a registered prediction
   cur_q = {pt, hit, ctr[1:0], tgt[19:2]}. It describes the instruction
   at the current PC.
     npc_seq = pt_q ? {pc_w[29:18], tgt_q} : pc_w + 1
               (flop select; reuse the existing incrementer)
     pc_w    <= redirect ? redirect_target[31:2] : npc_seq
     (same CE as today: redirect_ce || !stall)
     lookup  = btb.read(npc_seq): hit = tag == npc_seq tag,
               pt = hit && ctr[1]
     cur_q   <= redirect ? '0 : lookup   (same CE as pc_w)
   Effects:
   - The PC loop gains only a flop-selected 2:1 before the existing
     redirect mux, which can merge into one LUT5.
   - The BTB read path is PC -> +1 -> addr mux -> RAM -> compare ->
     !redirect AND -> flop. It ends at a flop and never feeds the PC in
     the same cycle.
   - A predicted-taken fetch looks up its own target during that cycle
     (npc_seq = tgt_q), so chains of taken transfers keep predicting.
   - Only the first instruction fetched after an EX redirect is
     unpredicted (cur_q is cleared). This costs 1 cycle only when that
     instruction is itself a taken branch or JAL, estimated at <0.5% of
     cycles.
   - It also makes liveness free: a replayed instruction is always
     refetched unpredicted, so r4s2's suppress_q flop is not needed.
   - PC advance and ID/EX capture share the same enable (no stall, or
     redirect with flush). So the pt latched into ID/EX is always the
     prediction that steered the PC.
   If the +1 carry into the tag bits turns out critical, compare the tag
   against pc_w[14:7] (un-incremented) on the sequential leg. A wrong
   tag at an index wrap only costs a mispredict.

3. ID (id_stage.sv) registers these into ID/EX, all derived from the
   cur_q flop plus the existing decode:
   - pt (kill bit, cleared on flush like br_ok), pred_tgt, hit, ctr.
   - br_inv <= funct3[0] ^ (pt && is_branch && !imm[1]). This folds the
     prediction into r4s0's existing
     cond = (use_lt ? lt : eq) ^ inv, as LESSONS suggests. For a
     predicted branch, cond then means "outcome != prediction", with no
     new EX level.
   - jal_ok <= is_jal && !imm[1] && !pt; jal_al <= is_jal && !imm[1];
     jalr_np <= is_jalr && !pt (kill bits).
   - alt_pc <= pt ? pc4 : pc_imm. This is the same depth as the existing
     pre_result mux after the pc_imm adder.

4. EX (ex_stage.sv), new terms computed only from ID/EX flops:
     tgt_ok = ({pc[31:20], pred_tgt} == pc_imm[31:2])
     bad_pt = pt && !((br_ok || jal_al) && tgt_ok)
     replay = bad_pt && (br_ok || jalr_k)   // wrong-target branch, any JALR
     jfix   = bad_pt && jal_al              // wrong-target JAL
     early  = jal_ok || bad_pt
     e_tgt  = replay ? pc : jfix ? pc_imm : alt_pc   // alt_pc = pc4 when pt
   Redirect stays one 4-input LUT after the compare, in both syn_keep
   copies:
     redirect = (br_ok && cond) || early || (jalr_np && !jalr_bit1)
     redirect_target = jalr_np ? {jalr_sum[31:1], 1'b0} : e_tgt
   This has the same shape as today's jalr ? jalr_sum : pc_imm, and the
   only late input is still jalr_sum.
   - Non-control instructions, br_bad and jal_bad with pt execute
     normally and redirect to pc4. There is no kill, so a mis-hit load,
     store or DIV is never replayed and div_stall needs no gating.
   - A replay (only branches and JALR, never memory ops or DIV) does:
     redirect to its own pc; set EX/MEM valid, reg_write and fwd_ok to 0
     as for the div bubble; replay is ORed into ex_wb_kill, next to the
     misalign_jump term that r3s1 and r4s0 already fold into the ID
     forward compare. The refetch is unpredicted (step 2), so progress
     is guaranteed.
   - The architectural next PC is RVFI-only and pruned in synthesis. It
     is recomputed as:
       (jalr_k && !bit1) ? jalr_sum
       : (jal_al || (br_ok && taken)) ? pc_imm
       : pc4
     where taken = cond ^ (pt && br_ok). The trap rules are unchanged
     (br_bad keeps the unflipped inv).

5. Training (core.sv to the BTB write port), fed only from EX/MEM flops:
   - EX/MEM carries: taken (late XOR into a flop only), is_br_al/jal_al,
     hit, ctr, a replay bit, and the existing branch_target = pc_imm.
   - taken branch or JAL: write
     {pc[14:7], pc_imm[19:2], JAL ? 11 : hit ? sat_inc(ctr) : 10}.
   - not-taken branch with a hit: sat_dec(ctr).
   - replay: write ctr = 00 at that index, so a stale entry cannot
     replay forever.
   - JALR is never trained.

Expected impact:
- Cycles: about -6% (r4s2 measured -6.44%, minus <0.5% for the unpredicted
  instruction after each redirect).
- Fmax: should stay at r4s0's ~104 MHz. The worst path (the EX ALU loop)
  is untouched, the redirect LUT keeps 4 inputs, and the new fetch path
  is registered.
- Fitness: about 232.94 * 1.06 = ~247 (+6%).
- Area: about +150 LUT4, +14 LUT-RAM blocks, +60 FF.

title: Operand-fanout diet plus a 2-level late-arrival result join on r4s0: one shared comparator, AGU folded into the ALU adder, adder joins last, MEM-stage regfile write
motivation:
The champion r4s0 (104.6 MHz median, 98.7 MHz on place option 0,
4,491,817 cycles) is limited by five tied ~10.1 ns families (r5s0's
probe of r4s0). Four of them start at the EX/MEM.alu_result bypass flop,
and a large share of each is routing on the bypass-mux output nets, not
logic:
  F1 DSP:      res -> 1.40 ns -> alu_b bypass LUT -> 1.67 ns (fanout 72)
               -> DSP -> mul_or -> out
  F2 adder:    alu_b bypass -> 2.05 ns -> sub carry chain -> 4 fast_or
               levels -> out LUT (5 LUTs after the chain)
  F3 regfile:  raw imem -> 4-level write-first compare -> fanout-32
               select -> rs2_res fwd mux -> ID/EX
  F4 SLT:      alu_b[1] bypass (fanout 77, 2.99 ns net) -> lt chain ->
               6 fast_or[0] levels -> out[0]
  F5 redirect: rs1 bypass (fanout 19) -> 32-bit eq tree + cond +
               redirect (7 LUTs) -> pc_w CE/D
EX currently has five 32-bit consumers on the bypass outputs that
duplicate each other: the ALU adder, the ALU subtractor, the ALU lt_s
and lt_u comparators, the separate branch br_lt comparator, the branch
eq on rs2, and a separate AGU adder rs1 + imm. For every LOAD, STORE and
JALR, alu_b already equals imm (alu_src = 1, so fwdb_ex = 0), so the
AGU sum equals the ALU adder's a + alu_b. For every branch, alu_b
already equals the bypassed rs2 (alu_src = 0, fwdb_ex = fwd2_ex), so
the branch compare can use the ALU's operands and comparator.
r5s0 tried to cut all five families and lost 8%, but its lesson names the
cause: two bad cuts (SLT moved into the final LUT after the DSP, and a
merged is_sub add/sub that did not map to one carry chain) plus
syn_keep on enable-loaded duplicate flops. This hypothesis keeps r5s0's
sound cuts, adds fanout removal, which nobody has tried, and avoids all
three failure modes.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Cycle count stays the same (4,491,817). All the gain is Fmax. Every cut
removes loads from a bypass net or LUT levels after a late arrival,
and nothing new is placed after the DSP product.

A. Fanout diet on the EX bypass nets (ex_stage.sv, alu.sv, id_stage.sv).
   1. One shared comparator: lt = $signed({a[31] & ~cmp_uns, a}) <
      $signed({alu_b[31] & ~cmp_uns, alu_b}), with cmp_uns a new
      registered ID/EX bit (1 for SLTU/SLTIU and for BLTU/BGEU via
      funct3[1], 0 otherwise). It replaces the ALU's lt_s, the ALU's lt_u
      and EX's br_lt. RS_SLT and RS_SLTU merge into one RS_SLT class
      (bit 0 = sel & lt). The ALU exports lt to ex_stage for branch_cond.
   2. Branch equality on the ALU operands: br_eq = (rs1 == alu_b). This is
      exact for branches (alu_src = 0, fwdb_ex = fwd2_ex), and branch_cond
      is gated by br_ok/br_bad anyway. The rs2 bypass mux then feeds only
      write_data / rs2_val (store data and RVFI).
   3. AGU folded into the ALU adder: jalr_sum := add_res (a + alu_b).
      This is exact for JALR/LOAD/STORE (alu_b = imm). It feeds
      EX/MEM.mem_addr, redirect_target (JALR), jalr_bit1 and mem_misalign
      exactly as today. The separate rs1 + imm adder is deleted.
   Net effect: the rs1 bypass output loses about 96 loads (AGU, 2
   comparators), alu_b loses about 64, and rs2 loses about 64. This
   shortens the 1.4-3.0 ns nets on F1/F2/F4/F5 and should let placement
   pull the DSP and carry chains closer.

B. Two-level late-arrival result join (alu.sv). Only r4s0's rule
   applies: at most two kept LUT levels follow a late unit.
     as_or    (syn_keep) = sel_add & add_res | sel_sub & sub_res  (1 LUT4)
     early_or (syn_keep) = logic, SLL, SR, DIV (quo_q), PRE, and on bit 0
                           only sel_slt & lt
     mul_or   (syn_keep) = unchanged (MULLO / MULHI, ALTOPS stand-ins)
     out                 = early_or | as_or | mul_or         (one LUT3)
   The adder chain then passes 2 LUTs (today 5). The DSP passes 2 LUTs
   (unchanged). lt passes early_or[0] and then out[0], 2 LUTs (today 6).
   Keep add and sub as two separate carry chains. No is_sub merge
   (r5s0 lesson). Do NOT put SLT into the final out LUT. If early_or is
   still deeper than the adder chain, split it into kept sub-ORs by
   arrival: flop-only div|pre first, then logic, then the shifters.

C. MEM-stage regfile write, no write-first compare (reg_file.sv, core.sv;
   r5s0's F3 cut, which was not the cause of its regression). The regfile
   write port is driven by the EX/MEM occupant: w_en = EX/MEM.fwd_ok (a
   flop, already reg_write && rd != 0 && !misaligned-jump && !mem-misalign,
   and 0 on bubbles), w_addr = EX/MEM.rd, w_data = mem_stage fwd_val. The
   read is LUT-RAM plus the x0 zero term only. The ID fwd_mem mux still
   covers the same-cycle writer. MEM/WB (I-3) is already in the RAM.
   During a dmem stall the held LOAD rewrites unready data each cycle. This
   is harmless: ID/EX is frozen and not flushed, and on the release cycle
   fwd_mem forwards the correct load data while the RAM is rewritten. Use
   an `initial` zero fill instead of the reset loop so Gowin keeps pure
   LUT-RAM. RVFI rd_wdata stays on the MEM/WB/wb_stage path (pruned in
   the timed netlist).

Process (r5s0 lesson: one bad cut hides the others). Implement A, then
B, then C, and run `make timing TARGET=bench` after each step. Keep a
step only if the place-option-0 Fmax does not drop and the top-path
families shrink. After the last edit, confirm in the timing report that
add_res/sub_res still come from single ALU carry chains. Also confirm that
no path goes through the DSP and more than mul_or -> out. Expected: all
five families lose 0.4-1.0 ns (fanout nets, plus 3 LUT levels on
F2/F4, plus the write-first compare on F3). That gives about
104.6 -> 110-113 MHz median at unchanged cycles, and about 2% fewer LUTs.

lesson: - 2026-09-30 hyp-20260930-001-r6s0 (regression, -1.61%): The operand-fanout diet (one cmp_uns-extended comparator shared by SLT/SLTU and the branches, br_eq on alu_b, the AGU folded into the ALU adder), the as_or/early_or/mul_or two-level result join and the MEM-stage regfile write cut LUTs from 2434 to 2157 and raised place option 0 from 98.7 to 103.3 MHz at unchanged cycles, but the scored median fell from 104.6 to 103.0 MHz: r4s0's option 0 sat about 6 MHz below its median, while here option 0 roughly equals the median, so the cuts mostly narrowed the spread across placement options instead of raising it, and option 0 ended on four families tied at about 9.7 ns that the ALU work left in place or created (rs1 bypass -> eq tree -> redirect -> flush_id -> ID/EX kill reset, DSP -> mul_or -> out, dmem rdata -> load extract -> fwd_val -> rs2_res -> op_b, and rs1 bypass -> shifter -> ~5-level early_or -> out[0]); so an option-0 gain is not a median gain, and every placement option should be timed before a cut is kept; also, folding the AGU into the ALU adder puts that carry chain on the JALR target -> pc_w path (it became the top path at 98.7 MHz when the shifters were split out of early_or).

title: Bypass-at-D: forward the EX result into the ID/EX operand flops, so EX runs on bare flops, with a MEM-stage regfile write (no write-first) to pay for the extra ID mux level
motivation:
On the champion r4s0 (median 104.6 MHz, place option 0 98.7 MHz, 4,491,817
cycles) every worst path is ~10.1 ns of data delay, and all the EX-side families
start the same way: EX/MEM.alu_result flop -> 1.2-1.4 ns net -> EX bypass
LUT (rs1 / rs2 / alu_b 2:1 mux) -> 1.7-3.0 ns high-fanout net (fanout 72-77)
-> consumer (DSP, add/sub chain, SLT chain, branch eq tree). Measured in
r5s0's probe of r4s0:
  F1 DSP:      alu_result -> 1.40 net -> alu_b LUT -> 1.67 net -> DSP -> mul_or -> out
  F2 adder:    alu_b bypass -> 2.05 net -> sub chain -> fast_or (4 lvls) -> out
  F4 SLT:      alu_b bypass (fanout 77, 2.99 ns net) -> lt chain -> fast_or[0]
  F5 redirect: alu_result -> rs1 bypass LUT (1.25 ns net) -> eq tree -> redirect -> pc_w
So in every EX family, one LUT level plus one long net (~1.7-2 ns, about 20% of
the period) is the bypass mux. r5s0 tried to cut these with micro-opts
(duplicate result flops, a 2-level OR, flop-sourced eq compares). It
regressed, because a new level after the DSP and the syn_keep CE-emulation
LUTs cancelled the gains. No attempt has changed where the bypass sits in the
pipeline. The mux can be moved to the other side of the ID/EX register
instead of being made faster.

Cycle behaviour stays bit-for-bit the same (same stalls, bubbles and

A. Bypass-at-D (ex_stage.sv, id_stage.sv, core_pkg.sv, core.sv).
   Today ID registers rs1_res / rs2_res / op_b and a registered fwd*_ex
   select, and EX muxes `fwd ? EX/MEM.alu_result : ID/EX.val`. Instead,
   apply the same select at the ID/EX D input, using EX's same-cycle result:
     ID/EX.rs1_val <= fwd1_ex ? ex_out : rs1_res
     ID/EX.rs2_val <= fwd2_ex ? ex_out : rs2_res
     ID/EX.op_b    <= (fwd2_ex && !alu_src) ? ex_out : op_b
   where ex_out is the ALU `out` (fast_or | mul_or) of the current ID/EX
   occupant, exported from ex_stage. fwd*_ex is the existing same-cycle
   compare in forward_unit (ID/EX.rd vs. raw rs fields, qualified by
   reg_write && !ex_wb_kill && rd != 0). EX then drops its three bypass
   muxes, and the ALU, DSP, branch comparator, AGU (rs1 + imm), write_data
   and divider start read ID/EX flops directly.
   Why it is exact: the value is captured only when ID/EX loads (!stall_id),
   which is the same cycle the producer moves EX -> EX/MEM. stall_id already
   covers dmem/div/load-use stalls, so the captured value equals the value
   EX/MEM.alu_result will hold, which is what the old mux would have
   selected. For a LOAD occupant, load-use holds the consumer. For a DIV
   occupant, capture happens only in the div_done && !stall cycle, when
   out = quo_q. On redirect/imem-stall flush the captured value is garbage
   in a killed slot, as today. The r2s1/r3s1 lockstep argument is unchanged,
   and no new late reg_write clear is added.
   Timing effect: the out LUT and the forward mux merge into one LUT4 per
   operand bit, {fwd, fast_or, mul_or, id_val}, or a MUX2_LUT5 whose select
   is fwd_ex. Each EX loop keeps the same number of LUT levels but loses the
   leading EX/MEM -> bypass-LUT net (1.2-1.4 ns) plus the LUT. F5 (redirect)
   loses the bypass LUT outright. The divider start is already flop-only.
   div_rs1_q / div_rs2_q become redundant: the held ID/EX flops are final
   values, so remove them and their EX/MEM muxes (64 fewer FFs).

B. Pay for the extra level on the ID side: regfile written from MEM with no
   write-first compare (reg_file.sv, core.sv, wb_stage.sv, forward_unit.sv).
   Moving the mux adds a level after rs1_res, on the ID path (lfsr imem ->
   4-level `w_en && w_addr == rs` write-first compare -> fanout-32 net ->
   2 LUTs -> ID/EX), which is itself ~10.1 ns. Remove that compare:
   w_en = EX/MEM.fwd_ok, w_addr = EX/MEM.rd, w_data = mem_stage fwd_val.
   This is the value ID already forwards through fwd*_mem. I-2 is then
   covered by fwd_mem in the same cycle it writes, and I-3 is already in the
   RAM, so the read is RAM plus the x0 term. During a dmem stall the held
   LOAD rewrites its rd each cycle with not-ready data. That is harmless:
   ID/EX is frozen (stall_id, flush gated off), and the completing cycle
   both rewrites the correct value and forwards it through fwd_mem. r5s0
   already implemented this exact write scheme and passed formal and cosim.
   The ID operand function becomes
   D = fwd_ex ? ex_out : (fwd_mem ? mem_fwd_val : rf), 5 inputs, which maps
   to 2 LUT4 + MUX2_LUT5 with fwd_ex on the MUX2 select. The ID path is then
   2 compare levels + 1 LUT + MUX2, down from 4 + 2 LUTs today.
   RVFI rd_wdata still comes from MEM/WB via wb_stage (pruned in the timed
   netlist).

Rules from LESSONS kept: nothing new after the DSP except the existing final
LUT (r5s0). Use no syn_keep on enable-loaded duplicate flops (r5s0). If
duplicating ID/EX operand flops to split the 72-77 fanout (e.g. a DSP-only
op_b / rs1 copy that Gowin can absorb into the MULT input register), use
syn_preserve and time it separately. Keep the r4s0 fast_or / mul_or late join
and the redirect_e PC-CE duplicate.

Estimate: the EX families lose ~1.2-1.6 ns of ~10.1 ns. The ID and dmem
paths gain at most a MUX2_LUT5 (~0.3 ns) after B removes 2 compare levels.
Median Fmax goes from ~104.6 to ~112-116 MHz at identical cycles, about
+7-10%.
Implementation order (from the r5s0 lesson): do A alone and run
`make timing`, then add B and time again, and keep B only if it helps. If the
new worst path is the dmem -> load-extract -> fwd_mem -> MUX2 -> ID/EX path,
pre-register mem_to_reg into the mem_fwd_val select, or feed load data into
the LUT4 input next to the MUX2 rather than in front of it.

Export ex_out (the ALU out = fast_or | mul_or) for the ID/EX D-input mux. Remove div_rs1_q/div_rs2_q and their is_div muxes (ID/EX holds the final operands while DIV waits). lesson: - 2026-09-30 hyp-20260930-002-r6s1 (regression, +0.79%): Bypass-at-D (EX's same-cycle `ex_out` muxed into the ID/EX rs1/rs2/op_b D inputs so EX reads bare flops, div_rs*_q dropped, 555 FFs) together with the MEM-stage regfile write raised place option 0 from 98.7 to 103.1 MHz, but fitness rose only 0.79%, because taking the bypass off the EX loops moved the clock-setting path to the ID/EX D side: all top-5 option-0 paths became dmem BSRAM read -> load extract -> mem_fwd_val -> rs2_res -> ID/EX op_b (8-9 cells, ~15 ns), the family r6s0 had already found tied at the limit, which now also passes through the fwd_ex select; the first build reached only 92.1 MHz, because Gowin shared logic across the three D muxes and rebuilt op_b as `alu_src ? imm : rs2_d`, which added a level on both the EX and ID paths until syn_keep was put on rs1_res/rs2_res/fwdb_ex; so a mux can be moved onto the ID/EX D side only after the load-forward path has slack (feed load data into the final LUT beside the fwd_ex select, or pre-register the mem_to_reg select), and because A and B were timed only together, it is unknown which one helped.

title: Look-ahead BTB on r4s0 with every new EX/PC input a flop: 30-bit registered target, kept next-PC net, ID-side target check
motivation:
r5s2 ported r4s2's 32-entry look-ahead LUT-RAM BTB onto the r4s0 champion.
It kept the whole IPC gain: 4,205,461 cycles vs 4,491,817 (-6.38%). It
still missed the 4.6% bar (239.04 vs 243.66) because Fmax fell from
104.63 to 100.53 MHz on placement options 1 and 2. The worst path was
EX/MEM alu_result -> pc_w[22], 11 cells. pc_w[22] lies in the pc_w[29:18]
range, where r5s2's npc_seq spliced the current PC
(pt_q ? {pc_w[29:18], tgt_q} : pc_w+1). Gowin folded that hold into the
PC clock enable, which put a LUT after redirect.
r5s2 also added logic to the EX redirect cone: a 30-bit ID/EX tgt_ok
compare, then bad_pt and early, and a 3-way e_tgt mux ahead of the
jalr_sum mux. These were flop-sourced, but they arrive at about the same
logic depth (4-5 LUTs) as the branch condition through the bypass. So
they compete with it in the redirect -> pc_w cone, which in r4s0 is
already one of the tied ~10.1 ns families.
The IPC side of this predictor is proven twice (r4s2 and r5s2, both
-6.4%). The remaining task is to build it so that the pc_w flop and the
EX redirect/target cone are structurally identical to r4s0's. At 4.205M
cycles, fitness beats the bar at any Fmax >= 102.5 MHz. At r4s0's
104.6 MHz it reaches about 248.8 (+6.8%).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Start from r4s0 (the current RTL). Re-implement r5s2's look-ahead BTB
with the same predictor semantics, so cycles should be about 4.205M.
Change three structural rules so that every signal the BTB adds to the
EX->redirect->PC loop is a single flop:

(A) Full-width registered predicted target. Do the splice before the
    flop. At lookup time register
      cur_q = {pt, hit, ctr[1:0], tgt30}
      tgt30 = {npc_seq[29:18], ram_tgt[17:0]}
    Then
      npc_seq = pt_q ? tgt30_q : pc_w + 1
    This has no pc_w hold leg, so synthesis cannot fold it into the CE.
    Mark npc_seq `(* syn_keep = 1 *)` (a comb net, not a flop).
    The PC flop then stays exactly r4s0's:
      pc_w <= redirect ? redirect_target[31:2] : npc_seq
    with CE = redirect_ce || !stall.
    cur_q uses the same CE. Its D is redirect ? '0 : lookup(npc_seq).
    Lookup: index npc_seq[4:0] (address bits [6:2]), 8-bit tag
    npc_seq[12:5] (address bits [14:7]), pt = hit && ctr[1]. Do not use
    a constant for the upper target bits, so Gowin has nothing to fold
    into the flop SR/CE pins.

(B) Target check in ID, not EX. In the IF/ID cycle, compute
      pred_off = tgt30_q - pc_w
    This is a 30-bit subtract from two flop groups, in parallel with
    the imem read. ID then computes
      tgt_ok = (pred_off == imm[31:2])
    This equals pc_imm == pred_tgt, but hangs off imm_gen instead of
    after the pc+imm carry chain, so it sits beside ID's existing
    imm -> adder -> pre_result path.
    ID registers these kill bits (cleared on flush like br_ok):
      bad_pt  = pt && !(((is_branch || is_jal) && !imm[1]) && tgt_ok)
      early   = (is_jal && !imm[1] && !pt) || bad_pt  // replaces jal_ok
      replay  = bad_pt && ((is_branch && !imm[1]) || is_jalr)
      jfix    = bad_pt && is_jal && !imm[1]
      jalr_np = is_jalr && !pt                        // replaces jalr_k
    Also register:
      br_inv <= funct3[0] ^ (pt && is_branch && !imm[1])
      alt_pc <= pt ? pc4 : pc_imm
    br_inv folds the prediction into the existing
    cond = (use_lt ? lt : eq) ^ inv.
    Clear ctrl.reg_write in ID/EX when replay is set. A replayed JALR
    then drops out of the ID-side fwd_ex compare with no new late
    reg_write clear, which keeps r2s1/r3s1's pre-decoded forward bits
    exact without touching ex_wb_kill.

(C) EX keeps r4s0's cone shape exactly. Both syn_keep copies are:
      redirect = (br_ok && cond) || early_q || (jalr_np && !jalr_bit1)
    This is r4s0's cone with jal_ok -> early_q and jalr_k -> jalr_np,
    both flops.
    The target is:
      e_tgt (syn_keep) = replay_q ? pc : jfix_q ? pc_imm : alt_pc
      redirect_target  = jalr_np ? {jalr_sum[31:1], 0} : e_tgt
    e_tgt is 2 levels from ID/EX flops, and the final mux has r4s0's
    is_jalr ? jalr_sum : pc_imm shape.
    On replay_q, EX/MEM valid, mem ops and fwd_ok are killed from the
    flop, as for the div bubble. Replays happen only on branches and
    JALRs, so never on a mem op or DIV. The refetch is unpredicted
    because cur_q is cleared on redirect, which also guarantees liveness.
    A non-control instruction with a false pt executes normally and
    redirects to pc4.
    The RVFI pc_next is the architectural next PC, is RVFI-only, and is
    pruned in synthesis.

Training is the same as r5s2, written from EX/MEM flops only:
- taken branch or JAL: allocate or increment (JAL ctr = 11, miss = 10)
- not-taken hit: decrement
- replay: clear ctr
- JALR: never trained.

Process rule, from LESSONS r5s0 and r5s2:
- Run `make timing` after the LAST RTL edit.
- List the top ~20 paths. None may end at pc_w, cur_q or ID/EX alt_pc,
  tgt_ok or early with more cells or arrival than r4s0's ~9.56 ns
  ALU-loop family.
- If one does, fix that path. If an ID path (imem -> imm ->
  pred_off compare) is on top, move the compare to use a registered
  pred_off. That costs nothing, because tgt30_q and pc_w are both
  flops one cycle earlier, as in the look-ahead.

Expected impact:
- Cycles: about 4.205M (-6.4%, as measured twice).
- Fmax: 103-105 MHz, because the pc_w D/CE cones and the EX redirect
  cone match r4s0 input for input.
- Fitness: about 246-249 (+5.5 to +7%).
- Area: about +180 LUT4, +14 RAM16, +100 FF.

title: Comparator-carry-last PC next-state and shifter late join for the median-setting paths
motivation:
I re-timed champion r4s0 on all three placement options (make timing
--all-options). The median 104.633 MHz comes from options 1 and 2,
which are identical. Option 0 sits alone at 98.7 MHz. So the scored
number is set by option 1/2's worst paths, and no previous round has
reported them. Two families are tied there:
  (a) 14.852 ns, 32 cells, the top 3 paths:
      EX/MEM alu_result_6 -> rs1 bypass LUT -> 26-cell carry chain
      (the br_lt 33-bit comparator) -> redirect_d_s8 -> redirect_d_s3
      -> redirect_d_s1 (fanout 32) -> u_if/n6_s0, the CE LUT
      (redirect_ce | !stall, fanout 30) -> pc_w CE.
      After the carry-out come four LUT levels, about 3.8 ns including
      nets. syn_keep on redirect_e did not keep the CE separate:
      n6_s0 is fed by redirect_d_s1.
  (b) 14.841 ns, 5 cells: alu_result_17 -> alu_result_9. A shift by
      8, so this is the bypass -> barrel shifter -> fast_or AND-OR ->
      out loop.
Option 0 adds rf -> ID/EX rs2_val (15.417 ns) and alu_result -> pc_w
(15.39 ns), both within 0.03 ns of its 5-cell ALU loop.
Lesson r4s0/r5s0: when the worst paths form tied families, a single-family
fix gains almost nothing, so this cuts (a) and (b) together. Neither
changes cycles (4,491,817 stays).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Cut (a): make the comparator carry-out the last-but-one LUT input into
pc_w, and drop the PC clock enable.
  - ID registers four branch kill bits, all cleared on flush:
      blt_t = br_ok & use_lt & !inv,  blt_f = br_ok & use_lt & inv,
      beq_t = br_ok & !use_lt & !inv, beq_f = br_ok & !use_lt & inv.
    (br_bad still sets the trap as before.)
  - EX builds two kept (syn_keep) redirect halves:
      r_lt   = lt ? blt_t : blt_f.
        This is a single LUT3 right after the carry-out.
      r_rest = eq ? (beq_t | oth) : (beq_f | oth),
        where oth = jal_ok | (jalr_k & !jalr_bit1) is kept and
        early-arriving.
    redirect = r_lt | r_rest keeps feeding flush_id / pc_next /
    ex_mem exactly as today.
  - if_stage: pc_w has no CE. D is one LUT4 per bit:
      pc_d[i] = (r_lt | r_rest) ? tgt[i] : seq[i]
    Both inputs are kept:
      tgt = is_jalr ? jalr_sum[31:2] : pc_imm[31:2]
      seq = stall_if ? pc_w : pc_w + 1
    seq absorbs load-use/imem/dmem/div holds, off the redirect cone.
    The lt path goes from carry-out -> 4 LUTs -> CE to
    carry-out -> 2 LUTs -> D. That is about 1.5-2 ns off family (a).
    The eq path loses one level as well. The JALR sum path stays at
    carry chain -> 2 LUTs.
Cut (b): take the shifters out of fast_or.
  - The last stage of the SLL and SRL/SRA networks is pre-masked by its
    registered one-hot sel bit. These are the kept sll_m and sr_m.
  - out = fast_or' | mul_or | sll_m | sr_m is one LUT4 per bit.
    fast_or' is the old fast_or without the SLL/SR terms.
  - The shifter path skips fast_or's 2-3 levels.
  - The DSP product still passes only mul_or and the final LUT, which
    keeps r4s0/r5s0's rule that nothing new sits after the multiplier.
  - SLT stays inside fast_or'. r5s0's mistake was moving it into out.
Both cuts are logically identical rewrites of the same functions. The
kill bits keep the r2s1/r3s1 flush discipline. No new late reg_write
clear is added, so fwd_ok / ex_wb_kill are untouched.
The implementer must time every placement option after the last edit,
since an option-0-only gain is not a median gain (r6s0). If one cut does
not help, report which one.

lesson: - 2026-09-30 hyp-20260930-001-r7s0 (regression, -1.93%): Splitting r4s0's redirect into kept halves (r_lt = lt ? blt_t : blt_f, and r_rest) that drive a PC with no CE through a D LUT, and joining pre-masked sll_m/sr_m directly into `out`, first dropped the median to 96.8 MHz, because once the 33-bit `<` result fed a small kept LUT, Gowin rebuilt the compare as a 6-8 level LUT tree (syn_keep on br_lt did not prevent it), and speed came back only when the compare was rewritten as the borrow bit of a 34-bit subtraction; the shorter redirect->PC path then exposed redirect -> flush_id -> ID/EX kill-bit reset as the worst path, fixed by merging the early flush terms with the redirect halves in one kept LUT4; even so, the final build reached 102.6 MHz (r4s0: 104.6) at unchanged cycles, with options 1/2 now limited by two untouched paths tied at 15.04 ns: the 5-cell fwd1_ex -> ALU -> alu_result loop (probably the DSP multiply) and dmem -> load extract -> ID/EX op_b; so on Gowin, write every magnitude compare as an explicit subtraction carry-out, treat redirect's PC and flush fanouts as one family, and time the ALU-loop and load-forward families before spending another round on the redirect.

title: Move pipeline-boundary work to the consumer side: split EX/MEM result regs, registered lazy wrong-path kill, late-entry load forward
motivation:
r4s0 (232.94, median 104.6 MHz, 4,491,817 cycles) is Fmax-bound. Its
worst path is the EX loop alu_result -> alu_result (5 cells: bypass LUT
-> unit -> fast_or / mul_or -> `out = fast_or | mul_or` -> EX/MEM flop).
r6s0's option-0 timing found four families tied at about 9.7 ns once one
is cut:
  (1) EX/MEM bypass -> ALU/shifter/DSP -> result OR -> out -> EX/MEM flop,
  (2) bypass -> branch compare -> redirect -> flush_id -> ID/EX kill bits,
  (3) dmem rdata -> load extract -> fwd_val -> rs2_res -> op_b -> ID/EX,
  (4) DSP -> mul_or -> out -> EX/MEM flop.
Every micro-cut inside a stage (r5s0, r6s0, r6s1) moved the median by
about 1%, because it fixed one family and the others stayed tied. What
these families have in common is that each has one level that only exists
because a merge is done on the *producer* side of a pipeline register,
before the flop: the final result OR, the same-cycle ID/EX kill, and the
mem_to_reg / fwd_mem / alu_src select chain in front of op_b. If each
merge moves across the register boundary into a LUT the consumer already
has, it costs no extra level there. This is a change to pipeline-register
contents and flush timing, so cycles and IPC stay identical.

  (1) EX/MEM bypass -> ALU/shifter/DSP -> result OR -> out -> EX/MEM flop,
  (2) bypass -> branch compare -> redirect -> flush_id -> ID/EX kill bits,
  (3) dmem rdata -> load extract -> fwd_val -> rs2_res -> op_b -> ID/EX,
  (4) DSP -> mul_or -> out -> EX/MEM flop.
Every micro-cut inside a stage (r5s0, r6s0, r6s1) moved the median by
about 1%, because it fixed one family and the others stayed tied. What
these families have in common is that each has one level that only exists
because a merge is done on the *producer* side of a pipeline register,
before the flop: the final result OR, the same-cycle ID/EX kill, and the
mem_to_reg / fwd_mem / alu_src select chain in front of op_b. If each
merge moves across the register boundary into a LUT the consumer already
has, it costs no extra level there. This is a change to pipeline-register
contents and flush timing, so cycles and IPC stay identical.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Three boundary moves, all with the same cycle count (the cosim cycle count
must stay at 4,491,817):

A. Split EX/MEM result, consumer-side OR (families 1 and 4).
   EX/MEM keeps two registered partials instead of alu_result:
     res_f_q = fast_or  (every non-multiply class, already masked by sel)
     res_m_q = mul_or   (MULLO / MULHI, already masked)
   They are kept as-is (syn_keep on fast_or / mul_or as today); the
   `out = fast_or | mul_or` LUT goes away. Consumers do the OR inside the
   LUT they already have:
     EX bypass:  rs1 = fwd1_ex ? (res_f_q | res_m_q) : in.rs1_val  (4-input
                 LUT4, the same one level as today; the same applies to rs2 /
                 alu_b)
     MEM fwd:    the ALU leg of fwd_val is res_f_q | res_m_q (from flops)
     MEM/WB:     alu_result <= res_f_q | res_m_q (from flops, off-path)
   So the ALU loop and the DSP path each lose one LUT level plus one
   routed net (about 1.0-1.3 ns of r4s0's ~9.6 ns period).
   Put (* syn_keep *) on the two EX/MEM partial flops' OR inside the
   bypass only if Gowin re-creates a separate OR level (check the netlist).

B. Registered lazy wrong-path kill (family 2).
   Remove `redirect` from flush_id. flush_id becomes
   (load_use || imem_stall) && !dmem_stall && !div_stall, and every input
   is a flop or a raw-imem compare. Add kill_q in ex_stage:
     kill_q <= redirect && !stall_id   (the wrong-path instruction entered
                                       ID/EX this edge); cleared otherwise
                                       when ID/EX loads; held when ID/EX holds.
   In EX, the ID/EX occupant is treated as a bubble when kill_q is set:
     - the redirect terms are pre-ANDed in parallel with the compare, from
       flops: brk = br_ok & !kill_q, jk = jal_ok & !kill_q,
       jrk = jalr_k & !kill_q (syn_keep), so
       redirect = (brk & cond) | jk | (jrk & !jalr_bit1) keeps today's
       5-input final LUT;
     - EX/MEM valid / reg_write / mem_read / mem_write / fwd_ok and the
       trap bits (br_bad, jal_bad, misalign) are gated with !kill_q on the
       EX/MEM D side (off-path);
     - is_div and div_start are gated with !kill_q;
     - ex_wb_kill (-> ID forward_unit ex_ok) ORs in kill_q, so the target
       instruction never forwards from the killed occupant;
     - hazard_unit's load-use compare is qualified with !kill_q (a flop) so
       a killed wrong-path LOAD cannot insert a bubble.
   The redirect net then drives only the pc_w CE / D mux and one kill_q
   flop, not the ID/EX kill-bit resets (valid, reg_write, mem_*,
   br_ok, ...). Cycle behavior is identical: the wrong-path slot is still
   a bubble and the target is fetched on the same cycle as today. This
   also covers the held-branch-during-dmem/div-stall case: kill_q is only
   set on an edge where ID/EX actually loads.

C. Late-entry load forward in ID (family 3).
   Register in EX/MEM two pre-qualified forward flags instead of one:
     fwd_alu_ok = fwd_ok && !mem_read,  fwd_ld_ok = fwd_ok && mem_read.
   forward_unit produces fwd{1,2}_alu / fwd{1,2}_ld from the raw-imem rs
   compares. mem_stage exports load_data (the extracted value) and the ALU
   value separately, not the merged fwd_val. ID builds
     op_b = ld2b ? load_data : (alu_src ? imm : (fwd2_alu ? alu_v : rs2_data))
   with ld2b = fwd2_ld && !alu_src precomputed from early signals, and
   rs1_res / rs2_res built the same way. This way the dmem BSRAM data
   passes only the byte/half extraction and one final mux LUT before the
   ID/EX flop, instead of extract -> fwd_val -> rs_res -> op_b. Pre-decode
   the extraction in EX from the AGU low bits (registered one-hot lane
   selects plus a sext-fill select in EX/MEM) so load_data is 2 LUT levels
   from rdata. Keep syn_keep on rs1_res / rs2_res / the load leg (r6s1
   showed Gowin re-sharing these muxes otherwise).

The three cuts are independent. Per LESSONS (r5s0, r6s0), time each cut
separately with `make timing` across all placement options if time allows,
and drop any cut that lowers the median. Formal and RVFI: RVFI is sourced
from MEM/WB, whose alu_result is rebuilt as res_f|res_m, so rd_wdata is
unchanged. A killed slot never reaches MEM/WB valid, so order / unique /
liveness keep their current shape.

title: Look-ahead BTB on r4s0 with redirect removed from the prediction flops (redir_q mask) and no new ID/EX kill bits
motivation:
The 32-entry look-ahead LUT-RAM BTB has been measured three times at the
same cycle cut: 4,491,817 -> 4,205,461 cycles (-6.38%, r4s2/r5s2/r6s2).
At 4.205M cycles it beats the 4.6% bar (243.65) at any median Fmax of
102.5 MHz or more. r6s2 reached 101.35 MHz (options 1/2) and 92.26 MHz
(option 0), against r4s0's 104.63/98.75.

r6s2's own scored worst path identifies the problem:
  cpu/u_ex/reg_q.alu_result_5 -> cpu/u_if/pt_q, 10 cells.
That path is EX/MEM bypass -> branch compare -> redirect -> cur_q.
r6s2 made pc_w's D/CE cone identical to r4s0's, but it registered the
prediction as `cur_q <= redirect ? '0 : lookup(npc_seq)` under the PC CE.
This adds about 34 new loads (pt, hit, ctr[1:0], tgt30[29:0]) to the
critical redirect net, plus one more LUT after redirect on the pt_q D
pin. The redirect net is the tail of r4s0's tied EX->redirect->PC
family, so doubling its fanout and giving it a new, deeper endpoint
costs exactly the ~3 MHz that r6s2 lost. r5s2's worst path was the same
family ending at pc_w[22].

A second, smaller cost: r6s2 added new ID/EX kill bits (early, replay,
jfix, jalr_np, pt, ...). These are all cleared by flush_id, and flush_id
is driven by redirect. r6s0 already listed
"rs1 bypass -> eq -> redirect -> flush_id -> ID/EX kill reset" as one of
r4s0's tied ~9.7 ns families, so every extra kill bit adds fanout there
too.

The predictor's IPC is proven. What remains is to keep the EX redirect
net's fanout and endpoints identical to r4s0's. Nothing the BTB adds
should load redirect or flush_id beyond one flop.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Start from the current RTL (r4s0). Re-implement r6s2's look-ahead BTB
with the same predictor semantics: 32 entries, direct-mapped, index
a[6:2], 8-bit tag a[14:7], 18-bit target a[19:2], 2-bit counter,
distributed LUT-RAM, async read, one sync write from EX/MEM flops, no
valid/reset. Use a Verilator-only `initial` zero fill. Training is as in
r5s2/r6s2: taken branch/JAL allocates or increments (JAL ctr = 11),
not-taken hit decrements, replay clears ctr, JALR is never trained.
Expected cycles stay about 4.205M. Change these structural rules:

(1) Take redirect out of the prediction flops. Keep r6s2's full-width
    registered cur_q = {pt, hit, ctr, tgt30}, with
    tgt30 = {npc_seq[29:18], ram_tgt}, but:
      - cur_q has NO redirect term in D and NO redirect_ce in CE:
          cur_q <= lookup(npc_seq)   with CE = !stall_if
      - add one flop redir_q ("cur_q does not describe pc_w"):
          redir_q <= redirect_d | (stall_if & redir_q)   (no CE)
        It is 1 after any cycle whose PC load was a redirect, and it
        holds while the PC holds.
      - pt_eff = pt_q & !redir_q (flops only, one LUT)
      - (* syn_keep *) npc_seq = pt_eff ? tgt30_q : pc_w + 1
      - pc_w stays exactly r4s0's:
          pc_w <= redirect ? redirect_target[31:2] : npc_seq
        with CE = redirect_ce || !stall
    Check all four cases:
      - redirect & stall: pc_w gets the target, cur_q holds stale,
        redir_q = 1 masks it.
      - redirect & !stall: cur_q gets lookup(npc_seq), which is the
        wrong address, and it is masked.
      - !redirect & !stall: pc_w and cur_q both advance to npc_seq,
        redir_q = 0.
      - hold: all three hold.
    The semantics match r6s2: the first fetch after a redirect is not
    predicted, which also guarantees liveness for replays. redirect_d
    gains 1 load instead of ~34, and the lookup chain
    (pc_w -> +1 -> npc_seq -> RAM16 -> tag compare -> pt_q) no longer
    has any EX input.
    Use pt_eff everywhere pt is consumed (ID kill-bit decode, pred_off).

(2) Add no new ID/EX kill bits. Keep flush_id's load set identical to
    r4s0's by renaming, not adding:
      - early replaces jal_ok. It is a kill bit, and it includes bad_pt.
      - jalr_np replaces jalr_k. It is a kill bit.
      - pt, replay, jfix and alt_pc become plain data fields. They are
        loaded when not stalled and are NOT cleared on flush.
    This is safe for these reasons:
      - replay and jfix only steer the syn_keep e_tgt mux, which matters
        only when redirect fires, and redirect needs early_q or the
        (killed) br_ok/jalr_np.
      - replay's EX/MEM kill (valid/mem ops/fwd_ok cleared from the
        flop) is idempotent on an already flushed slot.
      - pt only reaches EX through br_inv, which is qualified by the
        killed br_ok.
    Qualify replay in ID as `bad_pt && (is_branch && !imm[1] || is_jalr)`.
    Clear ctrl.reg_write in the ID/EX D when replay is set, as r6s2 did.
    That bit is already a kill bit, so the fwd_ex compare needs no new
    late qualifier.
    Training fields in EX/MEM follow the existing valid/kill.

(3) EX cone exactly as in r6s2/r4s0. Both syn_keep copies are:
      redirect = (br_ok && cond) || early_q || (jalr_np && !jalr_bit1)
    with cond = (use_lt ? lt : eq) ^ br_inv, and
    br_inv = funct3[0] ^ (pt_eff && is_branch && !imm[1]) folded in ID.
    e_tgt (syn_keep) = replay_q ? pc : jfix_q ? pc_imm : alt_pc
    redirect_target = jalr_np ? {jalr_sum[31:1], 0} : e_tgt

(4) ID target check as in r6s2:
      pred_off = tgt30_q - pc_w     (flop-sourced subtract in the IF cycle)
      tgt_ok   = (pred_off == imm[31:2])
    If timing shows imem -> imm_gen -> tgt_ok -> early among the top
    paths, register pred_off one cycle earlier from the lookup instead.
    Both operands are known when cur_q is written: pred_off_q =
    tgt30 - npc_seq, computed alongside the lookup under cur_q's CE.

Timing process (LESSONS r5s0/r6s0/r6s2):
  - Run `make timing` after the LAST RTL edit.
  - Report the top ~20 paths for every placement option, not only
    option 0.
  - Acceptance check before handing off: no path may end at pt_q/cur_q,
    redir_q, pc_w, ID/EX early/alt_pc, or the EX/MEM training fields
    with more cells than r4s0's EX->redirect->pc_w family.
  - If the BTB's own lookup chain (pc_w -> +1 carry -> npc_seq -> RAM16
    read -> 8-bit tag compare -> pt_q) is on top, split the compare:
    register the raw RAM tag and ctr[1] into cur_q, and do the 8-bit
    tag == npc tag compare against a registered copy of the looked-up
    npc tag bits in the fetch cycle. pt_eff is then 2 flop-sourced LUT
    levels, which is still far shorter than the EX redirect.

Expected impact:
  - Cycles: about 4.205M (-6.38%, same predictor semantics as r5s2/r6s2).
  - Fmax: about 103-104.5 MHz median. The redirect net and flush_id have
    r4s0's fanout plus one flop, and pt_q is no longer an EX endpoint.
  - Fitness: about 245-248 (+5 to +6.5%).
  - Area: about +170 LUT4, +14 RAM16, +60 FF (tgt30/pt/hit/ctr plus
    redir_q).

lesson: - 2026-09-30 hyp-20260930-003-r7s2 (regression, +4.55%): Taking redirect out of r6s2's look-ahead BTB prediction flops (cur_q <= lookup(npc_seq) under CE = !stall_if only, masked by one flop redir_q <= redirect_d | (stall_if & redir_q) as pt_eff = pt_q & !redir_q, which keeps the "first fetch after a redirect is unpredicted" liveness rule) and renaming instead of adding ID/EX kill bits (early/jalr_np replace jal_ok/jalr_k; pt/replay/jfix/alt_pc become unflushed data fields that only matter under a killed br_ok or early) scored 243.55, 0.1 below the 243.65 bar, so at the proven 4.205M cycles the implied median Fmax rose from 101.35 to about 102.4 MHz (the bar needed 102.5); this confirms that the ~34 extra redirect loads and the flush_id kill bits cost r6s2 about 1 MHz, but the three BTB ports (r5s2 100.5, r6s2 101.4, r7s2 102.4 MHz) have each recovered only ~1 MHz of a ~4 MHz loss, and now that the redirect load set is r4s0's plus one flop, the remaining ~2.2 MHz gap to r4s0's 104.6 MHz probably comes from what the BTB adds regardless of redirect, such as placement pressure from 14 RAM16s and ~300 extra LUTs (r6s2: 2751 vs 2434) or new branch_cond consumers in EX (br_taken_a = cond ^ (pt && br_ok) feeding the RVFI arch_next mux and the t_taken training flop, the kind of small extra consumer that made Gowin rebuild the compare as a LUT tree in r7s0); so keep r7s2's structure, stop trimming redirect, and find that last gap in r7s2's per-option timing report.

title: Cut both median-setting families of r4s0: DSP fed by its own operand flops (1-cycle fix-up only for EX-bypassed MULs) and a flattened load-forward leg into ID/EX
motivation:
r4s0 (232.94, cycles 4,491,817) sits at [98.7, 104.6, 104.6] MHz over the
three placement options; the median is set by options 1/2 at a 9.56 ns
period. Every later attempt that touched only one family moved the option-0
number and not the median (r5s0, r6s0, r6s1, r7s0). Where the option-1/2
paths were reported (r6s1, r7s0, both of which keep r4s0's EX loop and
load path unchanged), the median was set by two families tied at 15.04 ns
arrival:
  (a) EX/MEM.alu_result -> fwd1_ex/fwdb_ex bypass LUT -> ~1.7 ns
      high-fanout net -> DSP (3.76 ns combinational) -> mul_or -> out ->
      EX/MEM.alu_result (5 cells). The bypass LUT and its routing to the
      fixed DSP column cost ~2.2 ns of the 9.56 ns period.
  (b) dmem BSRAM rdata -> byte/half shift + sign-extend -> fwd_val
      (mem_to_reg) -> rs2_res (fwd2_mem) -> op_b (alu_src) -> ID/EX.op_b
      (8-9 cells), where every select is decoded after the BSRAM data arrives.
r6s1 found (b) alone was tied with (a), and r7s0 found them tied at the
same ns in its options 1/2, so, per the r4s0 lesson, both must be cut in
the same change or the median will not move.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Cycles stay unchanged except for +1 cycle on a MUL* whose operand comes
from the EX/MEM bypass (a MUL right after its non-load ALU producer; the
CoreMark matrix kernels feed MUL from loads, which already reach ID through
the MEM-stage forward after the load-use bubble, so this should be well
under 0.5% of cycles). The gain comes from Fmax.

A. DSP operand flops (family a). Add dedicated multiplier operand flops
   mul_a_q / mul_b_q (33-bit incl. sign-extension bit, computed from the
   ID-registered a_signed/b_signed), loaded on the same edge and CE as
   ID/EX.rs1_val / rs2 (not op_b: MUL is R-type) from the ID-resolved
   rs1_res / rs2_res, so Gowin can pack them into the DSP's input
   registers (A/B REG). prod = mul_a_q * mul_b_q; the DSP output joins
   only through the existing kept mul_or | fast_or join. No bypass LUT
   and no 72-fanout net in front of the DSP.
   Fix-up for the EX bypass: in ID, register mul_fix = is_mul && (fwd1_ex
   || fwd2_ex) (flop only, like fwd*_ex). In EX, mul_stall = valid &&
   mul_fix && !mul_ph_q holds PC and ID/EX exactly like div_stall (OR it
   into div_stall so hazard_unit is untouched), puts a bubble into EX/MEM,
   and reloads mul_a_q / mul_b_q from EX's post-bypass rs1 / rs2 (a
   flop -> 2:1 -> DSP-reg path, short). mul_ph_q is set for one cycle; on
   the next cycle the MUL completes with the correct product. Latch rs1/rs2
   for RVFI as the divider already does (reuse div_rs*_q, load on
   mul_stall too) because the producer drains out of EX/MEM.
   Keep the D-mux of mul_a_q / mul_b_q in the same LUT as the fwd*_mem
   select (D = mul_ph_load ? ex_rs : fwd_mem ? mem_fwd_val : rf_data, a
   LUT4+MUX2 per bit) so the load-forward path into the DSP registers is
   no deeper than into ID/EX.rs*_val. Under RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS the
   mul_lo/mul_hi stand-ins must read the same operands the real product
   uses (mul_a_q/mul_b_q low 32 bits) so formal exercises the fix-up stall.
   mul_a_q/mul_b_q use the ID/EX CE (!stall_id) except in the fix-up cycle,
   so a dmem stall overlapping the MUL keeps them held; mul_ph_q stays set
   until ID/EX next loads (the MUL leaves EX), not just for one clock.

B. Flattened load-forward leg (family b).
   1. EX computes and registers into EX/MEM a one-hot load-format select
      from jalr_sum[1:0], mem_width and mem_sext: ld_w (word), ld_b0..b3
      and ld_h0/h2 lane selects, and ld_sx (sign-extend) — flops only, so
      MEM's extract is a pure AND-OR on rdata with no addr*8 shifter and
      no width case decode after the BSRAM.
   2. EX/MEM also carries a registered is_load (mem_to_reg && fwd_ok) and
      is_alu (!mem_to_reg && fwd_ok) pair. In ID, split the MEM forward:
      fwd2_ld = is_load_q && rd match, fwd2_alu = is_alu_q && rd match,
      and build op_b / rs2_res / rs1_res so load_data enters the LAST
      LUT beside the fwd select (rs2_res = fwd2_ld ? load_data :
      (fwd2_alu ? alu_result : rs2_data)); op_b's imm leg is pre-muxed
      with the non-load legs (alu_src ? imm : fwd2_alu ? alu_result :
      rs2_data) and the load leg joins last with sel = fwd2_ld && !alu_src.
      Put (* syn_keep *) on the pre-muxed non-load partials so Gowin cannot
      re-collapse them in front of the load data (the r6s1 lesson).
   3. mem_fwd_val is no longer a single net: ID sees alu_result and
      load_data separately, which removes one level from the BSRAM path.

Expected: both tied families lose ~1-2 LUT levels / ~1.5 ns; if nothing
else sits within 0.4 ns of 9.56 ns in options 1/2, median Fmax rises to
~109-112 MHz (+4.5-7%) at ~unchanged cycles. Implementer: time A and B
separately and together on every placement option (not only option 0),
and keep a cut only if it moves options 1/2.

lesson: - 2026-09-30 hyp-20260930-001-r8s0 (regression, -9.95%): Cutting r4s0's two tied option-1/2 families in one change (33-bit mul_a_q/mul_b_q DSP operand flops loaded in ID from rs1_res/rs2_res with a 1-cycle mul_stall fix-up ORed into div_stall for EX-bypassed MULs, plus a load/ALU-split MEM forward with registered one-hot ld_lo/ld_mid/ld_w/ld_f8/ld_f16 extract selects) scored 209.76, which even with +0.5% cycles implies a median of only ~94-95 MHz (r4s0: 104.6), so the loss is Fmax and not the fix-up stalls; no per-option or per-cut timing was reported, but the likely cause is that the two cuts collide, because A moves the DSP's operand source onto ID's rs1_res/rs2_res, which puts the dmem BSRAM -> load extract -> forward-mux net that B was shortening in front of 66 new flops and adds a fourth (ex_rs reload) leg to that mux; the load/ALU-split forward has now been part of two regressed bundles (r7s1: 97.1 MHz) and has never been timed alone, so do not hang a new consumer on the load-forward net in the same change that cuts it, and build and time the split forward by itself on every placement option before bundling it with anything.

title: Decoupled front end on a look-ahead BTB: 2-entry bypassable fetch queue whose entries carry fetch-time prediction checks
motivation:
Two cycle cutters have been measured on r4s0 (4,491,817 cycles, 104.63 MHz
median), and neither clears the 4.6% bar alone:
  - r5s1 decoupled front end (2-entry bypassable IQ): 4,348,100 cycles
    (-3.2%), 103.02 MHz, 236.94.
  - r7s2 look-ahead BTB: 4,205,461 cycles (-6.38%), 102.43 MHz, 243.55
    (the bar was 243.65).
imem-not-ready bubbles (~0.28-0.31 CPI) are the largest loss. The IQ can
hide them only with words banked during back-end stalls, and today every
taken redirect flushes those words (r5s1 lesson: "revisit the IQ only on
top of a BTB, where predicted-taken branches stop flushing it"). With the
BTB, predicted-taken branches/JALs no longer flush the queue, so banked
words survive about twice as long, and redirect bubbles (~0.12 CPI) mostly
go away. The effects compound instead of adding: the -3.2% IQ gain was
measured with a flush every ~8 instructions. Neither piece alone costs
more than ~2 MHz, and their new paths are separate: the IQ adds a mux on
the ID input, the BTB adds a lookup path on the PC side.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Rebuild the front end of r4s0 (current RTL) as a decoupled predictor +
fetch queue:

1. Look-ahead BTB, exactly as described in r7s2's hypothesis text in
   cores/bench/experiments/log.jsonl (the r7s2 RTL was not committed, so
   re-implement it from that text): 32 entries, direct-mapped, index
   a[6:2], 8-bit tag a[14:7], 18-bit target a[19:2], 2-bit counter,
   distributed LUT-RAM with async read and one sync write from EX/MEM
   flops, no valid bits. cur_q = {pt, hit, ctr, tgt30} with
   tgt30 = {npc_seq[29:18], ram_tgt} is registered from
   lookup(npc_seq), where (* syn_keep *) npc_seq = pt_eff ? tgt30_q :
   pc_w + 1. cur_q has no redirect term. redir_q <= redirect_d |
   (pc_hold & redir_q), and pt_eff = pt_q & !redir_q, so the first fetch
   after a redirect is never predicted (liveness). The ID/EX kill bits
   are renamed, not added (early replaces jal_ok, jalr_np replaces
   jalr_k; pt/replay/jfix/alt_pc are unflushed data fields). pt is
   folded into the registered branch inv bit
   (br_inv = funct3[0] ^ (pt && is_branch && !imm[1])), so the EX
   redirect cone and its fanout match r4s0 input for input. Training
   rules are as in r7s2 (taken branch/JAL allocates or increments,
   JAL ctr = 11, not-taken hit decrements, replay clears, JALR never
   trained). Wherever r7s2 uses stall_if for the BTB, use the new
   pc_hold = !(redirect_ce | (imem_ready & occ != 2)) instead.

2. 2-entry bypassable IQ between the PC/BTB and ID (as in r5s1): PC CE =
   redirect_ce | (imem_ready & occ != 2), with no load-use/dmem/div term
   on the PC. The ID input is the IQ head when occ != 0 (registered
   select), else the raw imem word. valid_id = q_valid0 | imem_ready.
   consume = !stall_id. On redirect, clear the IQ and drop that cycle's
   fetch. stall_if is deleted. The hazard unit compares load-use on the
   ID-input word. flush_id = (redirect | load_use | !valid_id) &
   !dmem_stall & !div_stall.

3. The structural glue that makes 1+2 cheap: each IQ entry carries the
   prediction state of its word, computed at fetch time from flops:
   {instr, pc30, pt, tgt_ok}. pt = pt_eff of the fetch cycle. tgt_ok is
   r7s2's target check, moved from ID to fetch, i.e.
   (pred_off_q == raw word's B/J imm[31:2]), where
   pred_off_q = tgt30 - npc_seq is registered next to cur_q under the
   same CE (r7s2's suggested fallback, so the 30-bit subtract never sits
   between the imem word and a flop; if timing instead shows the lookup
   path pc_w -> +1 -> npc_seq -> RAM16 -> subtract -> pred_off_q among
   the top paths, go back to r7s2's flop-sourced tgt30_q - pc_w in the
   fetch cycle). The same fetch-time logic drives
   both the entry D input and the bypass leg of the ID mux, so a
   bypassed word and a banked word look the same to ID. ID then runs
   r7s2's early/replay/jfix/alt_pc decode unchanged, except that it
   reads pt/tgt_ok from the ID-input bundle instead of
   pt_eff/pc_w/tgt30_q. So the IQ mux is the only level added on the ID
   input path, and the BTB adds no 30-bit compare after it. Replay
   (bad prediction) works as in r7s2: re-steer to pc with the next
   prediction masked by redir_q.

Forwarding stays exact: ID/EX, EX/MEM and MEM/WB still advance in
lockstep (stall_id covers every dmem and div stall). Only the PC, the BTB
lookup and the IQ move independently, and forwarding reads none of them.
No new late reg_write clear is added. RVFI pc_wdata still comes from the
resolved next PC in EX/MEM.

Expected cycles: BTB -6.38% (measured) plus IQ. The IQ's -3.2% was
measured with a flush on every taken redirect; with BTB-covered branches
no longer flushing, expect -3 to -4% on top, so ~4.03-4.08M cycles
(-9 to -10%). Expected Fmax: 101-102.5 MHz (r7s2 102.4; r5s1's worst
path was IQ v0_q -> decoder -> pre_result, 30 cells at r4s0's arrival,
so the combined design must keep the IQ mux as the only extra ID level).
Fitness = 10*Fmax/Mcycles, so ~101.5/4.05 -> ~250 (+7%).

Timing rules from LESSONS that the implementation must follow:
syn_keep on the next-PC net npc_seq and on the IQ-head select copies
(one copy drives the regfile read address / load-use compare, one drives
decode/imm). No new consumer of branch_cond other than the kept redirect
copies and the EX/MEM training flop. Write any magnitude compare as a
subtraction carry-out. Time all three placement options (the median is
scored) before and after each timing edit, and report per-option Fmax
with the worst endpoint of each option.

lesson: - 2026-09-30 hyp-20260930-002-r8s1 (regression, -6.01%): Combining r7s2's look-ahead BTB (243.55, 102.4 MHz) with r5s1's 2-entry bypassable IQ (236.94, 103.0 MHz) scored 218.93, below both parts and below r4s0, so if cycles fell at least to the BTB's proven 4.205M (the target was ~4.05M), the implied median Fmax (10*Fmax/Mcycles) is only ~88-92 MHz, a loss of 10 MHz or more when neither part alone cost more than ~2 MHz; the loss must therefore sit on paths only the glue added, and no per-option timing was reported to say which one: the spec's BTB CE = !pc_hold = redirect_ce | (imem_ready & occ!=2) reused the PC enable and so put redirect_ce back on the ~64 cur_q/pred_off_q prediction flops that r7s2 had taken off redirect, and the new pred_off_q = tgt30 - npc_seq chains the pc_w+1 carry, the kept npc_seq mux, a RAM16 async read and a 30-bit subtract carry in one cycle; so when composing two separately timed front-end parts, give the BTB flops their own redirect-free enable, keep the predicted-target check flop-sourced (r7s2's tgt30_q - pc_w), and time the composite on every placement option instead of assuming the parts' Fmax costs add.

title: r7s2 look-ahead predictor rebuilt as one tagless BSRAM BTB whose sync read replaces cur_q
motivation:
The look-ahead BTB's IPC gain is proven. Three builds all reached
4,491,817 -> 4,205,461 cycles (-6.38%). r7s2 took redirect out of the
prediction flops and scored 243.55 (median 102.4 MHz) against a bar of
243.65. Its option-1/2 worst path is the same 5-cell ALU loop that sets
r4s0's 104.6 MHz. The redirect load set is already r4s0's plus one flop.
So, as the r7s2 lesson says, the remaining ~2 MHz is most likely what
the BTB adds regardless of redirect:
  - 14 RAM16s and ~300 extra LUTs (2799 vs 2434) crowding the EX
    placement,
  - the 8-bit tag compare,
  - 34 cur_q flops with their CE and D muxes.

An ISS trace of the timed CoreMark region (2.92M instructions) shows:
  - 294K taken branches, 49K JAL, 13.7K JALR (all returns);
  - 6.6K taken control transfers directly after a redirect;
  - so a return stack or other JALR prediction is worth at most ~0.3%
    of cycles and is not pursued.
The predictor lever left is to keep r7s2's semantics and remove the
BTB's fabric cost.

  - the 8-bit tag compare,
  - 34 cur_q flops with their CE and D muxes.

An ISS trace of the timed CoreMark region (2.92M instructions) shows:
  - 294K taken branches, 49K JAL, 13.7K JALR (all returns);
  - 6.6K taken control transfers directly after a redirect;
  - so a return stack or other JALR prediction is worth at most ~0.3%
    of cycles and is not pursued.
The predictor lever left is to keep r7s2's semantics and remove the
BTB's fabric cost.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Start from the current RTL (r4s0). Re-implement r7s2's predictor
semantics and its EX/ID structure unchanged:
  - redir_q masking: pt_eff = pt & !redir_q, with
    redir_q <= redirect_d | (stall_if & redir_q);
  - early/jalr_np renamed kill bits, and pt/replay/jfix/alt_pc as
    unflushed data fields;
  - pt folded into br_inv;
  - ID pred_off = tgt - pc compared against imm, with the bad_pt
    replay;
  - JALR never predicted;
  - training from EX/MEM flops only.

Replace the LUT-RAM storage and the cur_q prediction register with one
Gowin BSRAM used as a synchronous-read RAM. Its read register is the
look-ahead flop.
  - Storage: 1024 x 18, tagless.
    - index = a[11:2];
    - word = {ctr[1:0], tgt16} with tgt16 = target a[17:2].
    - A full-width 30-bit target is formed after the read as
      {pc_w[29:16], tgt16}. The upper bits are known equal because the
      ID pred_off check verifies the whole target, and a mismatch just
      replays.
    - If the splice ever folds into pc_w's CE (r5s2's failure), store
      a 30-bit target instead: 1024 x 32 = two BSRAMs, or 512 x 36.
  - Read: `if (!stall_if) rd_q <= mem[npc_seq[9:0]]`, using the BSRAM
    read CE. This is r7s2's `cur_q <= lookup(npc_seq)` with CE =
    !stall_if, minus the tag compare.
  - Prediction:
      pt = rd_q.ctr[1] & !redir_q
      (* syn_keep *) npc_seq = pt ? {pc_w[29:16], rd_q.tgt16}
                                  : pc_w + 1
    pc_w's D/CE cone stays exactly r4s0's and r7s2's.
  - Write: one synchronous port, from the EX/MEM training flops only
    (taken branch/JAL: tgt and ctr up; JAL ctr = 11; not taken: ctr
    down; replay: ctr = 0).
  - No reset and no valid bit. Any stored content is safe because the
    ID check replays a wrong target and EX verifies direction. Add a
    Verilator-only `initial` zero fill.

Why this should recover the Fmax r7s2 lost:
  - It removes 14 RAM16s, the 8-bit tag compare, 34 cur_q flops and
    their muxes (about 250-300 LUTs) from the fabric around EX.
  - The lookup loop becomes BSRAM clock-to-out -> 1-2 LUTs (pt/npc_seq
    mux) -> BSRAM address setup and the pc_w D mux, with no EX input.
  - With 1024 entries, the direct-mapped conflict misses mostly go away.
    A trace model of the timed region (2.92M instructions) counted the
    bubbles left from taken control transfers:

      - 32 entries, 8-bit tag: 67.9K (matches the measured -286K

      - 128 entries: 57.8K.

    aliasing is 4 KB apart and is caught by the existing replay.
