lesson: - 2026-09-30 hyp-20260930-003-r8s2 (regression, +3.37%): Moving r7s2's look-ahead BTB into one tagless 1024x18 BSRAM whose synchronous read register replaces cur_q (removing the 14 RAM16s, the 8-bit tag compare and the 34 cur_q flops) scored 240.78, below r7s2 (243.55) and even r6s2 (241.00), so either the implied median Fmax (10*Fmax/Mcycles) fell to about 101 MHz at the proven 4.205M cycles or cycles rose about 1.2% at r7s2's 102.4 MHz; no cycle count or per-option timing was reported to say which, but both candidates are new costs of the swap itself: a same-cycle BSRAM clock-to-out -> npc_seq mux -> BSRAM address setup loop (the read data selects its own next read address, through block RAM in fixed columns away from the PC logic), and tagless aliasing, which the trace model never simulated (it modeled only tagged tables) even though in the ISS build the hot list code (0x414-0x9c0) and matrix_test (0x168c-0x1bc0) overlap modulo 4 KB, and which, unlike a tag miss, turns an aliased instruction into a bad_pt replay that also zeroes the real branch's counter; so shedding ~300 LUTs of BTB fabric did not recover r7s2's ~2 MHz gap to r4s0, four BTB ports with different storage and redirect structure have now landed at 100.5-102.4 MHz, and the next predictor attempt should model every storage change (aliasing included) in the trace model before building it and look for the remaining gap on a path all the ports share, such as r7s2's scored alu_result -> redirect -> flush_id -> ID/EX ctrl.is_jump kill path (11 levels), not in the table.

title: Take the DSP off the EX bypass loop: flop-fed multiplier operands with a load-free ID source and a 1-cycle fix-up
motivation:
r4s0 (232.94, median 104.633 MHz) is set on placement options 1 and 2 by
a 5-cell EX/MEM.alu_result -> EX/MEM.alu_result loop (alu_result_8 ->
alu_result_15, 9.56 ns). Bit 8 -> bit 15 in 5 cells is the multiplier
loop: EX/MEM flop -> fwd1_ex/fwdb_ex bypass LUT -> 33x33 DSP ->
mul_or -> out -> EX/MEM D. r1s1 (3-cycle MUL), r4s1 (MUL in MEM) and
r8s0 (operand flops bundled with a load-forward split) all lost, but
none of them removed the bypass LUT from in front of the DSP while
keeping the load-forward net untouched: r8s0 hung 66 new flops on
rs1_res/rs2_res, i.e. behind dmem BSRAM -> load extract -> fwd_val,
the other tied family.

hypothesis.motivation:
r4s0 (232.94, median 104.633 MHz) is set on placement options 1 and 2 by
a 5-cell EX/MEM.alu_result -> EX/MEM.alu_result loop (alu_result_8 ->
alu_result_15, 9.56 ns). Bit 8 -> bit 15 in 5 cells is the multiplier
loop: EX/MEM flop -> fwd1_ex/fwdb_ex bypass LUT -> 33x33 DSP ->
mul_or -> out -> EX/MEM D. r1s1 (3-cycle MUL), r4s1 (MUL in MEM) and
r8s0 (operand flops bundled with a load-forward split) all lost, but
none of them removed the bypass LUT from in front of the DSP while
keeping the load-forward net untouched: r8s0 hung 66 new flops on
rs1_res/rs2_res, i.e. behind dmem BSRAM -> load extract -> fwd_val,
the other tied family.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Feed the multiplier only from dedicated operand flops mul_a_q / mul_b_q
(33 bits each incl. the sign-extension bit, so a_signed/b_signed also
leave the DSP input) that are loaded in ID at the same time as ID/EX,
from a source that never includes the dmem load-extract net:
  mul_a_d = fwd1_mem ? ex_mem.alu_result : rs1_data   (regfile, write-first)
  mul_b_d = fwd2_mem ? ex_mem.alu_result : rs2_data
(EX/MEM.alu_result is a flop, rs*_data is the LUT-RAM read that already
feeds rs1_res). A registered mul_fix bit is set in ID for a MUL/MULH*
whose operand comes from the EX bypass (fwd1_ex / fwd2_ex) or from an
I-2 LOAD (fwd*_mem && ex_mem.mem_to_reg). In EX, such a MUL raises
div_stall-style for exactly one cycle (reuse the existing div_stall path
into hazard_unit so no new stall term reaches the PC CE: mul_stall is a
flop-only AND of valid & mul_fix & !mul_fixed_q), during which
mul_a_q/mul_b_q reload from EX's post-bypass rs1 / rs2 (the same values
div_rs*_q latch today) and mul_fixed_q is set. The DSP path becomes
flop -> DSP -> mul_or -> out -> EX/MEM (one LUT and one route shorter),
and the ID-side load-forward path is unchanged (mul_*_d does not read
mem_fwd_val). mul_or stays a kept partial OR that joins last (r4s0 rule).
In CoreMark -O3 MULs are ~1-2% of dynamic instructions and only those
fed by the immediately preceding ALU op or an I-2 load pay the bubble,
so the cycle cost is estimated <0.5%. Expected: options 1/2 move off the
DSP loop onto the next family (base-ALU/shift loop or load-forward),
which r6s0/r7s0 put at ~9.2-9.4 ns, i.e. ~106-109 MHz median.
Implementation rules (from LESSONS): (1) this is a single cut; do not
bundle the load-forward split or any other change with it; (2) do not
add any consumer to mem_fwd_val / rs1_res / rs2_res / op_b; the new
flops read only fwd*_mem, ex_mem.alu_result and the regfile read;
(3) put the reload mux in front of mul_*_q only, never in front of
ID/EX rs*_val; (4) keep the sign-extension bit (a[31] & a_signed) in the
flop's D input, so nothing but flops feeds the DSP; (5) the ALTOPS
mul stand-ins must read the same mul_a_q/mul_b_q[31:0] so formal checks
the flop path; (6) the DSP-loop reading of alu_result_8 -> alu_result_15
(5 cells) is an inference, so first run `make timing` on the unchanged
r4s0 and confirm on every placement option that the DSP sits on the
median-setting path, then time the change on every option and report
per-option Fmax and the new top path.

Generate the 1-cycle mul fix-up stall from flops (valid & mul_fix & !mul_fixed_q), OR it into div_stall, bubble EX/MEM for that cycle, and export the post-bypass rs1/rs2 for the reload.
Multiply mul_a_q * mul_b_q directly (no a_signed/b_signed masking or bypass mux in front of the DSP); keep the fast_or/mul_or kept split and the ALTOPS stand-ins consistent.
Add mul_fix / mul operand fields to id_ex_t as needed.

lesson: - 2026-09-30 hyp-20260930-001-r9s0 (regression, -8.96%): Rebuilding r8s0's DSP operand flops as a single cut with a load-free ID source (mul_a/mul_b = fwd*_mem ? EX/MEM.alu_result : regfile read, sign-extension in bit 32, a 1-cycle div_stall fix-up for EX-bypassed or I-2-load operands, no new consumer on mem_fwd_val/rs*_res/op_b) scored 212.06, an implied median (10*Fmax/Mcycles) of only ~95-96 MHz at ~4.5M cycles, the same ~9 MHz loss as r8s0 (94.7 MHz), so r8s0's explanation that the load-forward split collided with the flops is wrong and the loss comes from ID-loaded DSP operand flops themselves; r8s0's reported top path (harness imem-data lfsr -> u_rf LUT-RAM read -> u_id mux -> u_alu/prod_65_s1, 9 cells) shows the likely mechanism: Gowin absorbs flops that feed only the DSP into the DSP block's input registers, so the cut does not add a clean pipeline stage but puts the raw-imem -> regfile read -> ID forward-mux path in front of a fixed-column DSP input register; with r1s1, r4s1, r8s0 and r9s0 all losing, keep r4s0's in-EX DSP with its late mul_or join, and any further attempt on the DSP loop must first confirm in the netlist that the new operand flops stay in fabric and time the D side of the DSP input on every placement option.

title: Decoupled front end rebuilt on r7s2's look-ahead BTB with redirect-free, flop-sourced glue (r8s1 done right, staged timing)
motivation:
Cycle budget of r4s0 (4.49M cycles, 2.92M instructions, CPI ~1.54, from r1s2/r5s1 traces):
imem-not-ready ~0.30 CPI, taken-redirect bubbles ~0.12, dmem stalls ~0.08, load-use ~0.06-0.10.
Fetch bandwidth is hard-capped at 0.78 words/cycle (xorshift ready is independent of requests),
so the only way to cut the dominant imem cost is to stop wasting *ready* fetch slots: (a)
wrong-path slots after taken transfers and (b) slots thrown away while the PC holds on back-end
stalls (load-use, dmem, DIV). Two measured parts do exactly this:
  - r7s2 look-ahead BTB (fixes a): 4.205M cycles (-6.38%), 102.4 MHz, 243.55 = +4.55%, missed the
    4.6% bar by 0.1 fitness point.
  - r5s1 2-entry bypassable IQ (fixes b): 4,348,100 cycles (-3.2%) at 103.02 MHz. Its gain was capped
    because every taken redirect flushed the banked words; with a BTB, predicted-taken transfers
    no longer flush the queue, so banked words survive ~2x longer and compound.
r8s1 composed them and crashed to ~88-92 MHz implied, but the lesson isolates the cause to the glue,
not the parts: (1) the BTB prediction flops (cur_q / pred_off_q, ~64 flops) reused the PC enable
redirect_ce | (imem_ready & occ!=2), putting redirect back on the flops r7s2 had taken it off, and
(2) pred_off_q = tgt30 - npc_seq chained pc_w+1 carry -> kept npc_seq mux -> RAM16 async read ->
30-bit subtract carry in one cycle. Neither is inherent to the composite.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Rebuild the composite so that every new net is either a flop or exactly one of the two proven
parts' own paths, and time it in two stages.

Base: re-implement r7s2 on r4s0 exactly as described in its log.jsonl hypothesis/implementation
notes (32-entry PC-indexed LUT-RAM BTB, 8-bit partial tag, look-ahead lookup of
npc_seq = pt_eff ? tgt30_q : pc_w+1 into cur_q, prediction flops CE = fetch advance only,
redir_q mask pt_eff = pt_q & !redir_q, pt folded into the registered br_inv, flop-sourced
target check pred_off = tgt30_q - pc_w vs imm in ID, bad_pt replay, renamed kill bits
early/jalr_np instead of added ones). STAGE 1: build only this, run `make timing` on every
placement option and confirm ~102 MHz median and 4.205M cycles before continuing. If it lands
well below, fix that first; do not add the IQ onto a broken base.

STAGE 2: add r5s1's 2-entry bypassable IQ between fetch and ID, with these rules (the r8s1 fixes):
  a. Two separate enables. pc_ce = redirect_ce | fetch_adv, where fetch_adv = imem_ready &
     (occ != 2) is a function of flops only (occ_q, imem_ready). The BTB lookup flops (cur_q,
     tgt30_q, pt_q, tag/hit flops) use CE = fetch_adv ONLY - never redirect_ce - and redirect
     reaches the predictor solely through the single redir_q flop:
     redir_q <= redirect_d | (!fetch_adv & redir_q). This keeps r7s2's "first fetch after a
     redirect is unpredicted" liveness rule and keeps redirect's load set = r4s0's + 1 flop +
     the IQ clear (occ_q, 2 valid bits).
  b. The predicted-target check stays flop-sourced: in the fetch cycle compute
     pred_off = tgt30_q - pc_w (flops -> one 30-bit carry chain) and store it, together with the
     word, pc, pt_eff and alt_pc bits, in the IQ entry when the word is banked. ID compares the
     entry's (or the bypass path's same-cycle) pred_off against imm_gen(ID word). Never subtract
     from npc_seq or from the RAM16 read data in the lookup cycle.
  c. ID input = registered-select 2:1 mux (occ_q != 0 ? IQ head : raw fetch bundle), exactly as
     r5s1; load-use/regfile address/forward compares read that mux output. stall_if disappears
     from the PC: back-end stalls (load-use, dmem, DIV) only stop consumption
     (consume = !stall_id) and let fetch bank words.
  d. Redirect (EX mispredict/replay/unpredicted taken) clears occ_q and drops that cycle's fetch;
     a predicted-taken transfer that verifies correctly does NOT flush the queue - this is the
     whole point of the composite.
  e. The hazard/forward lockstep invariant (lesson r2s1: ID/EX loads only when EX/MEM and MEM/WB
     advance) is untouched because the IQ sits entirely in front of ID.
After STAGE 2, time every placement option again. If the median drops more than ~1.5 MHz below
STAGE 1, list the new top-5 endpoints per option in implementation_notes and remove the
offending leg (do not retry with syn_keep blindly: lessons r5s0/r7s0 show kept LUTs can add
levels). Do NOT add a store buffer: in the timed wrapper dmem is a single-port async-read array,
so a drain mux on dmem_addr would sit on the already median-setting dmem -> load extract ->
fwd_val -> op_b path.

Expected: cycles ~4.03-4.10M (BTB 4.205M; the IQ's -3.2% was measured with a flush on every
taken redirect, so at least ~-2.5 to -4% more on top once predicted-taken transfers stop flushing
it). At a 100.5-102 MHz median that is 10*F/Mcycles = 245-253, i.e. +5 to +8.5% over r4s0
(232.94); break-even against the 4.6% bar is ~99.5 MHz at 4.08M cycles.
Report the exact cycle count and per-option Fmax for both stages.

title: Half-size r7s2 look-ahead BTB: 16 entries, 7 RAM16s, 20-bit target with no pc_w splice, to recover the placement-pressure Fmax gap
motivation:
r7s2's look-ahead LUT-RAM BTB is the best predictor so far. It scored
243.55 (bar 243.65) at the proven 4,205,461 cycles and a median of
102.4 MHz. Its per-option timing shows where the loss is:
  r4s0: opt0 98.75 MHz (5 cells), opt1/2 104.63 MHz (10 cells)
  r7s2: opt0 98.77 MHz (11 cells), opt1/2 102.43 MHz (5 cells)
The median-setting options 1/2 are no longer limited by any BTB or
redirect path. They are limited by the same 5-cell EX/MEM bypass ->
DSP/ALU -> alu_result loop that limits r4s0's option 0. That loop was
under 9.56 ns in r4s0's options 1/2 and is 9.76 ns in r7s2's. r8s2 shows
the same pattern (5 cells, 101.25 MHz).
So the ~2 MHz is placement pressure: the BTB adds ~365 LUT4, 14 RAM16s
and ~140 FFs near EX, and the DSP loop gets a worse placement. It is
not logic depth; three ports already trimmed redirect depth and gained
only ~1 MHz each.

Trace data (reference ISS, timed region, 2.92M instructions):
  - Taken branch/JAL/JALR bubbles with no BTB: 357,527.
  - r7s2 model (32 entries, 8-bit tag, look-ahead, no prediction on the
    first fetch after a redirect, JALR untrained, replay clears the
    entry): 69,741 bubbles left, a 287.8K saving. The hardware measured
    286.4K (4,491,817 -> 4,205,461), so the model is calibrated.
  - 16 entries, 8-bit tag: 81,930 left (+12.2K cycles, +0.29%).
  -  8 entries: 119K (+1.2%). 64 entries: 65K (-0.1%).
  - 16 entries, 4-bit tag: 93K (+0.56%). Tagless is far worse at every
    size (16: 246K), which confirms r8s2's aliasing loss.
  - JALR is only 13,735 dynamic instructions (all returns, 0.33% of
    cycles), so RAS or JALR prediction is not worth any logic.
A 16-entry, 8-bit-tag table keeps 96% of r7s2's cycle cut with half the
RAM16s and a narrower prediction/target datapath.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Start from the current RTL (r4s0). Re-implement r7s2 exactly as its
log.jsonl hypothesis specifies (id hyp-20260930-003-r7s2): the
look-ahead cur_q lookup with CE = !stall_if and no redirect term; the
redir_q mask, with pt_eff = pt_q & !redir_q; the kept npc_seq mux; pc_w
D/CE identical to r4s0; pt folded into br_inv; the early/jalr_np renames
of jal_ok/jalr_k, so no new ID/EX kill bits; pt/replay/jfix/alt_pc as
unflushed data fields; replay qualified as
bad_pt && (is_branch && !imm[1] || is_jalr); training only from EX/MEM
flops; JALR never trained. Change only the storage and target width.

(1) 16 entries, direct-mapped. Index pc[5:2], tag pc[13:6] (8 bits),
    2-bit counter. Keep the r5s2/r6s2 training rules: a taken branch
    allocates or increments, a JAL sets ctr = 11, a not-taken hit
    decrements, a replay clears ctr.
(2) The target stores only word-address bits [19:2] (18 bits). Code
    lives below 0x00100000, so the predicted 30-bit word target is
    {12'b0, ram_tgt}: constant zeros, NOT spliced from pc_w or npc_seq.
    A wrong guess (only possible with code >= 1 MB) is caught by the
    existing ID pred_off check and replayed, so correctness and the
    liveness rule (first fetch after a redirect is not predicted) are
    unchanged.
    Entry = 8 tag + 18 target + 2 ctr = 28 bits. That is 16x28 = seven
    RAM16SDP4, down from 14. cur_q stores {pt, ctr, tgt18}; drop
    tgt30_q's 12 upper flops. npc_seq[29:18] = pt_eff ? 0 : inc[29:18]
    (one AND per bit, kept syn_keep like the rest of npc_seq).
    pred_off = {12'b0, tgt18_q} - pc_w against the sign-extended imm,
    as in r7s2, but with a zero upper operand.
(3) Keep every r7s2 timing rule. Keep syn_keep on npc_seq and on both
    redirect copies. Add no loads on redirect or flush_id beyond r4s0's
    plus redir_q. Write magnitude compares as subtract carry-outs (r7s0
    lesson). Keep the fast_or | mul_or late DSP join intact.

Expected: cycles ~4.218M (+0.29% vs r7s2's 4.205M, -6.1% vs r4s0).
With roughly half the BTB fabric, the ALU/DSP loop in options 1/2
should regain ~1-1.5 MHz, to 103.5-104 MHz. That gives
10 * 103.5e6 / 4.218e6 = 245.4 (+5.3%), or 246.6 at 104 MHz. The bar
(243.65) needs a median of at least 102.8 MHz at 4.218M cycles.
Before submitting, time all three placement options and report each
option's worst path. If options 1/2 are still on the 5-cell DSP loop
below 103 MHz, report that. It would show that the gap is not area but
a single extra consumer on the EX/MEM alu_result or bypass nets (e.g.
the training flops or br_taken_a = cond ^ (pt && br_ok)), which should
then be moved to flop-sourced EX/MEM-stage logic.

title: Put the LUT-ripple PC incrementers and the LUT-tree branch compare on Gowin carry chains, and give the shifter its own kept partial OR
motivation:
Fresh `make timing TARGET=bench` on the champion r9s2 (place option 0,
101.5 MHz, 1014 violating endpoints) shows five path families tied
within 0.2 ns at ~9.8 ns data delay. Three of them are synthesis
artifacts, where Gowin built arithmetic as LUT chains:
  1. pc_w[1] -> pc_w[18] D (10 levels): `inc = pc_w + 30'd1` was NOT
     mapped to an ALU carry chain. The report shows a 9-LUT ripple
     "all-ones prefix" chain (npc_seq_4_s2 -> _7_s2 -> _10_s2 -> _11_s2
     -> _14_s2 -> _16_s2 -> _18_s3 -> _18_s4 -> n122 -> D), 0.4-0.97 ns
     of routing between each pair. The same thing happens to ID's
     `pc4 = in.pc + 4`: paths 5/17/18 run pc_w[1] -> pre_result[27] /
     alt_pc[19] / pre_result[19] (8 cells).
  2. EX/MEM alu_result -> rs1 bypass -> redirect_d -> flush_id -> ID/EX
     kill-bit RESET (early, valid, br_ok; 11 levels) and the same cone
     into the pc_w CE (paths 13-15, 25). The branch compare is a 7-LUT
     tree (redirect_d_s48 -> s30 -> s12 -> s7 -> s5 -> s3 -> s1), the
     same LUT-tree rebuild of `<` that r7s0 saw. r9s2's logged
     median-setting options 1/2 end on an 11-cell path, which matches
     this family and not the 5-cell DSP loop.
  3. alu_result -> rs1 bypass -> shifter (n54_s4, n54_s2) -> four
     fast_or levels (fast_or_30_s6/_s3, fast_or_14_s2/_s1) -> out
     (9 levels): the barrel shifter enters at the bottom of the
     10-term fast_or tree.
The other two are real: the DSP loop (alu_result_31 -> mul_a_32 ->
DSP 3.76 ns -> mul_or -> out, 5 cells) and dmem DO -> load extract ->
ID/EX rs2_val/op_b. The DSP loop is the floor: at ~9.8 ns in option 0
and at or below 9.42 ns in options 1/2, where r9s2's 106.13 MHz median
was set by an 11-cell path. Trace data puts load-use at ~0 under -O3,
and the BTB already recovers 96% of taken-branch bubbles, so Fmax is
the only micro_opt lever left. As r4s0 showed, every tied non-DSP
family has to be cut at once.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Make three local cuts, one per artifact family. Cycles, pipeline
structure and the BTB stay unchanged.

A. PC incrementers on a carry chain, one shared adder.
   - In if_stage, write the sequential increment as a real two-operand
     add so Gowin maps it to an ALU carry chain, not a LUT ripple. Use a
     non-constant carry source: a flop `run_q <= !reset` (it is 0 only
     during reset, when pc_w is forced to RESET_PC anyway), then
     `inc = pc_w + {29'b0, run_q}`. If the netlist still shows LUT
     chain cells (npc_seq_*_s2), put `(* syn_keep *)` on inc.
     30 ALU cells cost ~1.5-2 ns, against ~7.5 ns for the 9-LUT ripple.
   - Export inc to ID as a new if_id_t field `pc4w` (= pc_w + 1, the
     word address of pc + 4). ID's `pc4` becomes {in.pc4w, 2'b00},
     which removes ID's second 30-bit incrementer. pre_result/alt_pc
     then see one carry chain plus their existing mux (paths 5/17/18).
   - npc_seq stays kept, and pc_w's D/CE structure is unchanged.
B. Branch compare as a carry-chain borrow (r7s0 rule).
   - In ex_stage, replace the `$signed(...) < $signed(...)` branch
     compare with the borrow of an explicit subtraction:
       br_sub = {{2{rs1[31] & ~br_uns}}, rs1} - {{2{rs2[31] & ~br_uns}}, rs2};
       br_lt  = br_sub[33];
     Mark br_sub `(* syn_keep *)` so it cannot be rebuilt as a LUT tree.
     Keep br_eq = (rs1 == rs2) (a 3-level tree). Leave branch_cond,
     both kept redirect copies, flush_id and the pc_w CE split unchanged.
   - Apply the same rule to the ALU's lt_s / lt_u: take them from
     sub_res's carry chain as one 33-bit `{1'b0,a} - {1'b0,b}` borrow
     plus sign fix-up, lt_s = (a[31] ^ b[31]) ? a[31] : borrow, and
     lt_u = borrow. They join fast_or as before.
C. Shifter as its own kept partial OR.
   - In alu.sv, move RS_SLL and RS_SR out of fast_or into a new
     `(* syn_keep *) sh_or = ({32{sel[RS_SLL]}} & sll_res) |
     ({32{sel[RS_SR]}} & sr_ext[31:0])`, then
     out = fast_or | sh_or | mul_or. The final LUT is a LUT3, so the
     DSP still sees exactly one LUT after mul_or (r5s0's rule: nothing
     new in series after the DSP). fast_or loses two of its ten terms
     (one fewer OR level), and the shifter no longer enters at the
     bottom of that tree.

Expected: families 1-3 drop from 9-11 levels to about 5-7. The
median-setting options 1/2 then move up to the DSP loop floor
(~9.2-9.4 ns in those placements): about 106 -> 109-111 MHz median at
~4.216M cycles, i.e. +3 to +5%. Area drops slightly (one incrementer
and LUT trees removed), which also relieves the placement pressure
that r9s2 showed matters here.

lesson: - 2026-09-30 hyp-20260930-001-r10s0 (regression, -3.53%): Three cuts chosen from an option-0-only timing report (a kept `pc_w + {29'b0, ~reset}` carry-chain incrementer shared with ID's pc4, a kept 34-bit br_sub borrow for the branch compare plus SLT/SLTU from the SUB borrow, and SLL/SR moved into a kept sh_or joined as fast_or | sh_or | mul_or) raised place option 0 from 101.5 to 103.7 MHz at unchanged cycles, but options 1/2 fell from 106.1 to 102.4 MHz (with 21 more LUTs, not the expected area drop), and the compare, now on carry cells, still ties the DSP loop and dmem -> rs2_val as a 37-cell rs2 bypass -> carry chain -> pc_w path; in all 28 logged runs options 1 and 2 returned identical Fmax, so the scored median is always option 1's value and option 0 never counts, and because option 0 can differ from option 1 by up to 9 MHz (r6s2: 92.3 vs 101.4) and here moved the opposite way, choose and verify every Fmax cut on option 1's timing report, not option 0's.

title: Squash-in-EX control + 2-entry fetch queue on r9s2's 16-entry BTB, with the queue select moved after the BTB target check
motivation:
The BTB + 2-entry IQ composite has a proven cycle cut: r8s1 and r9s1 both
logged 4,011,459 cycles, -4.9% vs the champion r9s2 (4,215,892). A
predicted-taken branch no longer flushes the queue, so words banked
during back-end stalls hide imem-not-ready cycles (22% of cycles from the
xorshift generator, independent of the core). Both composites lost only
Fmax, and their logged worst paths show two separate families that the
IQ lengthened:
  r8s1 (87.8 MHz): ID/EX fwd1_ex -> EX bypass/branch compare -> redirect
    -> flush_id -> ID/EX jalr_np kill bit (38 cells). flush_id carried
    IQ terms behind the EX redirect.
  r9s1 (92.2 MHz): IF occ_q -> IQ head mux -> imm_gen -> pred_off
    equality -> bad_pt -> ID/EX (25 cells). The queue select sits in
    front of the imm format mux and the 30-bit target compare.
r5s1 (IQ without the BTB check) lost only 1.6 MHz vs r4s0. At 4.011M
cycles the composite needs ~105.6 MHz median to clear the 4.6% bar
(champion: 106.1 MHz), so both families must stay off the new logic.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Start from r9s2 (current RTL). Three structural changes, built together
because the cycle cut needs all of them, but timed stage by stage.
(1) Squash-in-EX. EX's redirect drives only pc_w (D mux + kept CE copy),
redir_q, the IQ valid bits, and one new flop squash_q <= redirect &&
!stall_ex_mem. flush_id loses its redirect term:
flush_id = (load_use || !fetch_valid) && !dmem_stall && !div_stall.
The wrong-path word that ID/EX captures in the redirect cycle is killed
one cycle later in EX: redirect_d/redirect_e, EX/MEM valid, reg_write,
mem_read/mem_write, fwd_ok, t_jal/t_br/t_clr, div_stall/div_start and
the load-use compare are each ANDed with !squash_q (one flop input on an
existing AND). ID's fwd*_ex compare adds !squash_q to ex_ok. The dead
slot is in ID/EX in the same cycle the old flush bubble was, so cycle
counts are unchanged; the redirect -> flush_id -> ID/EX kill family
disappears.
(2) 2-entry bypassable fetch queue (r5s1 structure). PC CE =
redirect_ce | (imem_ready && occ != 2). BTB cur_q flops keep their own
enable = fetch_adv; redirect reaches the predictor only through redir_q.
Each IQ entry banks {pc, instr, pt, hit, ctr, tgt_ok}.
(3) Queue select after the target check. tgt_ok is computed twice:
raw_tgt_ok from io_imemData and the flop-sourced pred_off = tgt18_q -
pc_w, and bank_tgt_ok computed when the word is written into the queue
and stored with it. Both use direct B/J immediate field compares
(eqB = pred_off == immB[31:2], eqJ = pred_off == immJ[31:2], tgt_ok =
isB&eqB | isJAL&eqJ), with no imm_gen format mux in front. ID uses

(1) and (3)) and a median of 104-107 MHz, for about +3% to +6%.

lesson: - 2026-09-30 hyp-20260930-002-r10s1 (regression, -2.83%): Rebuilding the BTB + 2-entry IQ composite on r9s2 with squash-in-EX (redirect drives only pc_w, redir_q, the IQ valid bits and a squash_q flop, so flush_id loses its redirect term) and a tgt_ok computed before the queue select (raw from imem, banked per entry, flop-selected 2:1 in ID) scored 244.62, so at the composite's ~4.01M cycles the implied median (10*Fmax/Mcycles) is ~98 MHz, up from r9s1's 92.2 and r8s1's 87.8; this confirms that both logged families (redirect -> flush_id -> ID/EX kill, occ_q -> IQ mux -> imm_gen -> pred_off -> bad_pt) were real, but the composite is still ~8 MHz below r9s2's 106.1, and the plan could not have cleared the bar anyway: a -4.9% cycle cut against a 4.6% bar leaves only ~0.5 MHz of Fmax budget (105.6 MHz needed), which is less than the IQ alone has ever cost (r5s1: -1.6 MHz on r4s0), and r9s2 showed that this core loses Fmax to added area near EX, where the IQ adds ~134 banked flops and squash_q adds loads on redirect_d/redirect_e and the bypass fwd_ok/ex_ok terms; so before building a composite, check that the parts' measured standalone Fmax costs fit inside the headroom its proven cycle cut leaves above the bar, and shelve BTB+IQ until the queue's cycle cut grows or the queue alone is shown to cost no Fmax.

title: Footprint-sized BTB: 14-bit target (6 RAM16s) and a 15-bit flop-sourced target check instead of the 30-bit pred_off subtract
motivation:
I re-timed the r9s2 champion on all three placement options (make timing
--all-options). Options 1 and 2 build the same netlist, so the median is
106.129 MHz. On those two options the top 8 paths are tied within 0.02 ns
(14.70-14.72 ns). None of them starts or ends in the BTB:
  fwd1_ex -> EX bypass -> ALU -> alu_result (23 / 26 / 8 cells),
  fwd1_ex -> branch compare -> redirect -> pc_w_16 (9 cells),
  dmem BSRAM -> load extract -> ID op_b / rs2_val (7-8 cells),
  fwd1_ex -> redirect -> flush_id -> ID/EX valid (10 cells).
Option 0 (101.5 MHz) ties pc_w -> +1 carry -> npc_seq -> pc_w with the
same ALU loops.
So the predictor's remaining cost to Fmax is placement pressure, not
logic depth, as r9s2's lesson concluded: halving r7s2's table
(-7 RAM16s, -12 target flops, about -120 LUTs) moved the median from
102.4 to 106.1 MHz even though no BTB path was critical in either
design. The IPC side has little left to gain: the calibrated trace model
leaves about 82K bubbles (1.9% of 4.216M cycles), and about 65K of those
are not capacity misses (JALR 13.7K, direction mispredicts). A bigger or
smarter table can win at most about 1%. The predictor can still help the
score by taking area away from the EX loops without losing its cycle cut.
Two parts of r9s2's BTB are wider than the CoreMark code footprint needs:
  - The 18-bit stored target covers 1 MB. CoreMark's hot code is at
    0x414-0x1bc0 and the whole image is well under 64 KB.
  - ID's target check pred_off = {12'b0, tgt18_q} - pc_w is a full
    30-bit subtract and a 30-bit equality against imm[31:2], placed
    beside imm_gen on the imem -> ID path.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Start from the current RTL (r9s2). Keep the look-ahead, the redir_q mask,
the training rules, pc_w D/CE, the kill bits, and the redirect cone
exactly as they are. Change only the stored width and the target check.

(1) Target field = word-address bits [15:2] (14 bits). Entry =
    {tag[7:0], tgt[13:0], ctr[1:0]} = 24 bits = exactly 6 RAM16s (now 7).
    The predicted word target is {16'b0, tgt14_q}. Constant zeros, not
    spliced from pc_w, per the r5s2 lesson. In the kept npc_seq,
    bits [29:14] become inc & ~pt_eff (they are [29:18] now). Training
    writes branch_target[15:2]. tgt18_q becomes tgt14_q (4 fewer
    flops). A target at or above 64 KB mispredicts and is caught by the
    replay in (2). Liveness is unchanged, because the first fetch after
    a redirect is still never predicted.

(2) Narrow, flop-sourced target check. With the stored target
    T = {16'b0, t14}, a prediction for pc (word) is correct iff
    pc + imm_w == T (mod 2^30). Split this into:
      - hi_ok = (pc_w[29:14] == 0). This is a 16-input NOR from the PC
        flops, off the imem path. Register it with the other
        prediction bits if that is easier, since pc_w is loaded
        together with cur_q.
      - d15 = {1'b0, t14} - {1'b0, pc_w[13:0]}. This is a 15-bit
        flop-sourced subtract, replacing the 30-bit one.
      - tgt_ok = hi_ok && (imm[16:2] == d15) &&
                 (imm[31:17] == {15{d15[14]}}).
    If pc and T are both below 64 KB, then pc + imm_w == T iff
    imm_w == sext(d15). So tgt_ok is exact whenever hi_ok holds. When
    hi_ok is false, tgt_ok = 0 and the prediction replays. That is
    safe (bad_pt path) and never happens in CoreMark. From imm_gen's
    output the depth is the same as today (bit equalities, then an AND
    tree). About 15 carry cells and about 15 XOR/eq LUTs go away.
    if_id_t.pred_off shrinks to 15 bits, plus a hi_ok bit.

(3) No other changes. Do not add new consumers on redirect, flush_id,
    fwd1_ex, mem_fwd_val, or the EX/MEM bypass. Do not touch the ALU,
    the forwarding, or the hazard logic.

Expected effect: cycles unchanged (about 4.216M; only code at or above
64 KB would change behavior). About 1 RAM16, 4 FFs and 30-40
LUT/ALU cells come off the front end. The gain depends on placement.
Before keeping the change, the implementer must run
`python3 -m tools.eval.gowin bench --all-options` and report per-option
Fmax and the top paths. If no option moves, the change is neutral and
should be reported as such. If (2) adds a level to any imem -> ID/EX
path that shows up in the option-1/2 top paths, keep (1) only and keep
the 30-bit pred_off check. Report which one was kept.

Kept npc_seq[13:0] = pt_eff ? tgt14_q : inc[13:0], npc_seq[29:14] = inc[29:14] & ~pt_eff. Export pred_d15 = {1'b0,tgt14_q} - {1'b0,pc_w[13:0]} and hi_ok = (pc_w[29:14] == 0) in place of the 30-bit pred_off. Everything else (look-ahead lookup, CE = !stall, redir_q mask, pc_w D/CE) is unchanged.

tgt_ok = hi_ok && imm[16:2] == pred_d15 && imm[31:17] == {15{pred_d15[14]}}; bad_pt/replay/early are otherwise unchanged.
t_wdata = {ex_mem.pc[13:6], ex_mem.branch_target[15:2], t_ctr_new} (24 bits); widen/narrow the t_wdata port to match.

tgt_ok = hi_ok && imm[16:2] == pred_d15 && imm[31:17] == {15{pred_d15[14]}}; bad_pt/replay/early are otherwise unchanged.

lesson: - 2026-09-30 hyp-20260930-003-r10s2 (regression, -4.82%): Narrowing r9s2's BTB target from 18 to 14 bits (6 RAM16s instead of 7, 4 fewer target flops, npc_seq[29:14] = inc & ~pt_eff) but keeping the 30-bit pred_off check (the narrow hi_ok/d15 check in part (2) was not built, and no reason or timing was reported) scored 239.61, so at r9s2's unchanged 4,215,892 cycles (all CoreMark code is far below 64 KB) the implied median (10*Fmax/Mcycles) fell from 106.1 to about 101.0 MHz from removing area alone; so r9s2's rule that a smaller predictor gives more Fmax is not monotonic: options 1 and 2 always build the same netlist, so the scored median is a single placement sample, and with its top 8 paths tied within 0.02 ns (fwd1_ex -> ALU -> alu_result, fwd1_ex -> redirect -> pc_w, dmem -> load extract -> op_b), a tiny netlist change can reshuffle placement and move Fmax by about 5%, more than any area trim can gain; part of r9s2's +8% may itself have been placement luck, so treat small area trims as placement noise rather than an Fmax lever, and spend Fmax effort on shortening the logic depth of those tied EX families.

title: Byte-lane replication of the high-fanout select nets that start or steer r9s2's tied EX, redirect and load-forward paths
motivation:
r9s2 (251.74, 106.1 MHz median, 4,215,892 cycles) has its top paths tied
within ~0.02 ns across three families (r10s2 lesson): (1) ID/EX fwd1_ex ->
EX bypass mux -> ALU/DSP -> result OR -> EX/MEM.alu_result, (2) ID/EX
fwd1_ex -> bypass mux -> branch compare -> redirect -> pc_w / flush_id kill
bits, (3) dmem BSRAM -> load extract -> mem_fwd_val -> rs2_res -> op_b /
rs2_val. Every depth cut tried since r5 (r5s0, r6s0, r7s0, r10s0) moved one
family and let another take over, or added a level somewhere else. What the
logged paths have in common is where they start or turn: families 1 and 2
START at a single registered select flop (fwd1_ex, and fwd2_ex/fwdb_ex on
the B side) that drives 32 bypass-mux LUTs plus the AGU/compare cones, so
the first hop of the worst path is a fanout-32+ net that the placer cannot
keep short around the DSP and carry columns. Family 3's turn points are
also wide nets: the load sign bit (selected from rdata[7/15/23/31]) fans
out to up to 24 upper bits, the EX/MEM mem_to_reg and mem_addr[1:0] selects
steer 32 bits each, and fwd2_mem (lfsr imem -> 5-bit compare) steers 64
LUTs (rs2_res + op_b). None of this changes logic depth, cycles, or the
predictor, so it is orthogonal to everything the lessons already rule out.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Keep r9s2's microarchitecture bit-for-bit (same cycles, 4,215,892) and
replicate only the select/turn nets on the tied families so that no such
net drives more than ~8-16 LUTs:
  A. EX bypass selects: ID/EX fwd1_ex, fwd2_ex, fwdb_ex become four
     identical per-byte-lane flops each (fwd1_q[3:0], fwd2_q[3:0],
     fwdb_q[3:0]), declared as separate regs in id_stage with
     (* syn_preserve = 1 *) (NOT syn_keep: r5s0 showed syn_keep on
     enable-loaded flops adds a CE-emulation LUT in front of D). EX builds
     rs1/rs2/alu_b byte k from lane k's select. The D input is the existing
     single fwd*_ex compare result (the compare itself is not duplicated).
  B. ID MEM-forward selects: forward_unit produces fwd1_mem/fwd2_mem in two
     kept copies (low half / high half), each a separate 5-bit compare
     (* syn_keep *), so each drives 16 rs_res (+16 op_b) LUTs instead of 32
     (+32). ~8 extra LUTs.
  C. Load extract in mem_stage: the sign bit of LB/LH is formed by three
     kept copies (one each for result bytes 1, 2, 3) of the small
     sign-select LUT (rdata bits 7/15/23/31, mem_addr[1:0], width, sext),
     so each copy fans out to 8 bits; ex_stage registers two extra
     (* syn_preserve *) copies of the mem_to_reg bit and mem_addr[1:0]
     (lanes low/high half) used only by the load-extract / fwd_val muxes,
     leaving EX/MEM.ctrl.mem_to_reg and mem_addr for everything else.
Area cost is about 12-20 flops and ~15 LUTs, far below the area swings
that r9s2/r10s2 tie to placement. If the first hop of families 1-2 drops
from a fanout-32+ route (~1.2-1.8 ns on GW2A) to a fanout-8 route
(~0.5-0.7 ns) and family 3 loses one wide-net hop, the tied frontier moves
by ~0.6-0.9 ns of a ~9.4 ns period, i.e. +5-9% Fmax at unchanged cycles.
The implementer must time on place option 1 (the scored median; r10s0
lesson) with `make timing TARGET=bench`, confirm in the Gowin netlist that
the duplicated flops and kept LUTs survived (distinct *_s0 instances, not
merged), and, if a part does not survive or does not move its family,
report that per part rather than bundling blindly (r5s0 / r8s0 lesson).
If a part pushes a different path to the top, drop that part and keep
the rest.

changes.description: Add (* syn_preserve = 1 *) logic [3:0] fwd1_q, fwd2_q, fwdb_q loaded under the same !stall CE as reg_q, each bit <= the existing fwd1_ex / fwd2_ex / (fwd2_ex && !dec_alu_src); export them as new output ports (the ID/EX struct fields fwd1_ex/fwd2_ex/fwdb_ex may be removed or left for RVFI-only use). Build rs1_res/rs2_res/op_b per 16-bit half from the corresponding kept fwd*_mem copy from forward_unit. Keep syn_keep on rs1_res/rs2_res as r6s1 recommends so Gowin cannot re-share the three D muxes.

Emit two (* syn_keep *) copies of fwd1_mem and fwd2_mem (lo/hi), each its own 5-bit rd compare qualified by ex_mem_fwd_ok, so each copy drives one 16-bit half of rs*_res/op_b. fwd*_ex outputs unchanged (single compare feeding the replicated ID/EX flops).

title: End every EX loop at a flop: registered redirect, MUL product in the DSP output register, and load/MUL results delivered to EX from a MEM/WB late_q leg
motivation:
r9s2 (champion, 251.74, 106.1 MHz median, 4,215,892 cycles) has its option-1
timing set by four tied families that all rerun inside a single cycle.
Every one of them already ends at the edge of what one cycle can hold:
  (1) EX/MEM.alu_result -> fwd1_ex bypass -> 33x33 DSP -> mul_or -> out ->
      EX/MEM.alu_result (r4s0's "5-cell" ALU loop; the DSP array alone is
      most of the period),
  (2) fwd1_ex bypass -> branch compare -> redirect -> pc_w D/CE and
      -> flush_id -> ID/EX kill bits (r8s2/r9s1/r10s1 logged paths),
  (3) dmem BSRAM -> load extract -> mem_fwd_val -> rs2_res -> op_b/rs2_val
      (top path of r6s0, r6s1, r7s0, r10s0, r10s2),
  (4) pc_w -> LUT-ripple +1 -> npc_seq -> pc_w (r9s2's logged worst path,
      10 cells) and the look-ahead BTB lookup hanging off npc_seq.
Ten rounds of micro-cuts show that the median Fmax does not move when only
one family is cut (r5s0, r6s0, r7s0, r10s0): another family ties at the
same ~9.4 ns and a small netlist change reshuffles placement by ~5%. An
Fmax gain large enough to clear the 4.6% bar needs a pipeline change that
takes the long part of every family out of its single-cycle loop, paid for
with a small, bounded number of cycles.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Restructure the pipeline so that the slow part of each loop ends at a flop,
accepting two small, well-measured cycle costs:

A. Registered redirect (resolve in EX, apply one cycle later).
   EX computes redirect_d / redirect_target exactly as today, but they
   only feed flops: redirect_q <= redirect_d && !stall_ex_mem, and
   redirect_tgt_q <= redirect_target. pc_w D = redirect_q ? tgt_q : npc_seq,
   pc_w CE = redirect_q | !stall_if, flush_id = redirect_q | load_use |
   imem_stall (gated as today), IF redir_q <= redirect_q | (stall & redir_q).
   The EX occupant during the redirect_q cycle is the wrong-path instruction
   that followed the branch, so it is squashed in EX: EX/MEM valid,
   reg_write, mem_read, mem_write, fwd_ok and t_jal/t_br/t_clr D inputs are
   ANDed with !redirect_q (a flop input on the D side only), redirect_d is
   gated by !redirect_q (a wrong-path branch never redirects), and is_div
   is gated by !redirect_q so a wrong-path DIV never starts. In the
   redirect_q cycle EX/MEM holds the branch (no mem op), so no dmem stall
   can coincide, and the pipeline always advances. BTB training becomes
   t_taken = t_pt ^ redirect_q (redirect_q is high exactly while the
   branch sits in EX/MEM). RVFI arch_next is still computed in EX from
   redirect_d, so pc_wdata is unchanged. Cost: 1 extra bubble per redirect
   (the trace model counted ~68-70K redirects with the 16/32-entry BTB,
   so about +1.7% cycles). Family (2) then ends at the redirect_q flop
   (bypass -> compare -> 1 LUT -> flop), and the PC D-mux select, the PC
   CE and the kill-bit flush are all flop-driven.

B. MUL* product registered in the DSP output register (late result).
   alu.sv drops mul_or from `out` (out = fast_or, one fewer level after
   the adder/shifter too) and registers the full 64-bit product (ALTOPS:
   the 32-bit lo and hi stand-ins) with no clock enable and no logic between
   the multiplier and the flop, so Gowin absorbs it into the DSP output
   register. The MUL moves to EX/MEM with alu_result = don't-care; the
   lo/hi pick happens after the flop, on the D side of MEM/WB.late_q.
   A MUL* is a "late" producer like a LOAD: hazard_unit's load-use
   compare uses id_ex_late = mem_read | is_mul, so a distance-1 consumer
   waits one cycle. CoreMark's timed region has ~94K MUL* (r1s1's +188.8K
   cycles for 2 extra stalls each), so the cost is at most +94K and more
   likely ~50K cycles (+1.2%). The DSP path becomes bypass LUT -> DSP ->
   DSP output register, with no mul_or/out LUTs and no fabric routing back
   to EX/MEM.

C. Late results (LOAD and MUL*) reach EX through one registered leg.
   MEM/WB.late_q <= is_mul ? (hi ? prod_q[63:32] : prod_q[31:0]) :
   load_data (all selects are EX/MEM flops). The MEM-stage forward to ID
   becomes flop-only: mem_fwd_val = EX/MEM.alu_result, and it is used only
   when the EX/MEM occupant is an early (non-late) producer
   (fwd_ok_early). When the EX/MEM occupant is a late producer and matches
   rs1/rs2, ID sets registered fwd1_late / fwd2_late / fwdb_late bits
   instead, and EX picks
     rs1 = fwd1_ex ? EX/MEM.alu_result : (fwd1_late ? late_q : rs1_val)
   with the inner 2:1 kept (syn_keep) as a flop-only LUT so the
   alu_result loop still passes a single mux LUT (let Gowin use a
   LUT4 + MUX2_LUT5 if it prefers; check which is faster on option 1).
   The load-use penalty stays at exactly 1 cycle for distance 1 and 0 for
   distance 2 (the consumer reaches EX when the load reaches MEM/WB), so
   this piece costs no cycles. MEM/WB is already held on dmem stall
   (hold_wb keeps data fields), so late_q stays valid while the consumer
   is held in EX. WB writes w_data = is_late ? late_q : alu_result.
   Family (3) disappears: dmem -> extract -> late_q is a short flop-to-flop
   path, and every ID -> ID/EX operand path loses the mem_to_reg mux and
   the dmem leg.

D. Carry-chain PC incrementer. With the redirect select now a flop,
   the only fetch-loop depth left is pc_w + 1; build it as a kept
   carry-chain add (r10s0's `pc_w + {29'b0, run_q}` form) so the pc_w ->
   npc_seq -> pc_w and npc_seq -> RAM16 -> tag compare -> pt_q paths
   shorten together. Keep r9s2's BTB, cur_q CE = !stall_if and redir_q
   masking unchanged.

Net: cycles about 4.216M * 1.03 = ~4.34M. The remaining loops are
bypass LUT -> 32-bit carry -> 2-3 level fast_or (about 6-7 levels),
bypass -> 33-bit borrow compare -> redirect_q, bypass LUT -> DSP -> DSP
output register, and the ID decode / regfile / pred_off paths from flops
(the imem LFSR and ID/EX), none longer than about 7-8 levels, so the median
should move from 106 MHz to roughly 118-122 MHz: fitness 10*F/4.34 =
272-281 (+8% to +12%). Break-even against the 4.6% bar is 114.3 MHz.
Implementation order matters: build and time A+C first (C costs 0
cycles), then add B and D, and report option-1 Fmax and the top path
after each step.

title: Private branch-resolve operand path: duplicated bypass selects and EX/MEM result copies for the predictor-check compare and JALR adder, off the ALU-loop nets
motivation:
After r9s2 the predictor has no IPC left worth chasing. The calibrated
trace model leaves about 82K redirect bubbles (1.9% of 4.216M cycles;
this pipeline has no IF/ID register, so a redirect costs 1 bubble).
About 17K are BTB capacity misses, 13.7K are JALR returns, and the rest
are direction mispredicts, mostly on data-dependent branches such as the
crcu8 parity branch that history cannot predict. A RAS or gshare could
recover at most about 0.5-1%, and a RAS would need a 30-bit JALR target
check on the redirect path. The stall generator is a free-running
xorshift that advances every cycle whatever the core does, so the ~22%
imem stalls cannot be predicted either. The predictor can only help the
score through Fmax, on the branch-resolve logic it owns.

r9s2's options 1 and 2 (the scored median, 106.1 MHz) have their top 8
paths tied within 0.02 ns, and every one starts at the same ID/EX
bypass-select flops and the same rs1/rs2 bypass-mux nets:
  fwd1_ex -> EX bypass -> ALU -> alu_result (23/26/8 cells)
  fwd1_ex -> branch compare -> redirect -> pc_w_16 (9 cells)
  fwd1_ex -> redirect -> flush_id -> ID/EX valid/jalr_np (10 cells)
  dmem -> load extract -> ID op_b / rs2_val (7-8 cells)
The shared start is the fanout, not the logic depth. fwd1_ex/fwd2_ex and
EX/MEM.alu_result each drive 32 mux LUTs, and the muxed rs1/rs2 nets then
feed the adder, subtractor, logic ops, both shifters, the DSP, the
branch eq tree, the 33-bit lt compare, the rs1+imm JALR/AGU carry chain,
the divider latch and the EX/MEM rs*_val/write_data flops. The branch
consumers (eq + lt + jalr_sum, about 100 LUT/carry loads) belong to the
predictor check: branch_cond already carries the prediction folded into
br_inv. They share nets with the ALU loop, so the placer has to put the
compare, the ALU and the PC logic around one set of wires. That is why
one ALU family, two redirect families and one PC family tie at the same
arrival time.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Give the branch-resolve / predictor-check logic its own operand path so
that the redirect cone and the ALU loop no longer share any net after
the ID/EX flops. Keep the predictor (the r9s2 16-entry look-ahead BTB,
pt folded into br_inv, flop-only early/replay/jfix/alt_pc) and every
cycle-level behaviour exactly as they are, so cycles stay at 4,215,892.

(1) ID registers duplicate bypass selects for the branch path:
    fwd1_br / fwd2_br (same value as fwd1_ex / fwd2_ex, separate flops,
    (* syn_preserve = 1 *) rather than syn_keep so that Gowin keeps its
    native DFFE CE and adds no CE-emulation LUT, per r5s0). They load
    under the same !stall enable as the rest of ID/EX.
(2) EX/MEM gets a second copy of the result, alu_result_br
    ((* syn_preserve = 1 *), same D as alu_result). It is read only by
    the branch-path bypass.

title: Shorter PC loop and load forward: a registered upper-PC +1 takes the 30-bit incrementer out of the pc_w loop, and one-hot load-lane selects flatten dmem -> ID/EX
motivation:
The champion r9s2 (251.74, 106.1 MHz, 4,215,892 cycles) logged its scored
critical path as cpu/u_if/pc_w_1 -> cpu/u_if/pc_w_18 (10 cells, 15.146 ns,
u_if only). That loop is pc_w -> 30-bit +1 (inc) -> kept npc_seq mux
(pt_eff) -> redirect D-mux -> pc_w, so the carry into bit 18 (an 18-input
AND / carry chain) sits inside a loop that nothing in EX, ID or MEM can
shorten. r11s0's lesson says to shorten this loop before the EX
families. The other family that has set the clock on r9s2-based builds
outside EX is dmem BSRAM -> load extract -> mem_fwd_val -> rs2_res ->
ID/EX rs2_val/op_b (r10s0 and r11s2 logged it, 7-8 cells, ~15 ns). It has
5-6 LUT levels after the BSRAM (4:1 shift mux, byte/half sign select,
sext mask, mem_to_reg mux, fwd2_mem mux, alu_src mux). The one-hot
load-lane forward has only ever been built inside bundles that regressed
for other reasons: r8s0's loss was later traced to its DSP operand flops
(r9s0). It has never been timed alone.
r11s2's lesson: on this base, rewiring or replicating nets is placement
noise. Only removing real logic levels can reach the ~111 MHz the 4.6%
bar needs. Both cuts below remove levels, and neither adds a load to the
EX bypass/ALU/redirect cone or area near EX.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Two independent depth cuts, both outside EX:

(A) Registered upper-PC increment. Split pc_w into lo = pc_w[5:0] and
hi = pc_w[29:6]. Add a free-running flop hi_p1_q <= pc_w[29:6] + 1 (a
flop-to-flop path with a whole cycle, not in the loop) and a flop
hi_stale_q, set when pc_w loaded a new hi on the last cycle, i.e. when
pc_w was enabled with redirect, with pt_eff, or with a lo carry. Otherwise
hi_stale_q <= 0 (a held PC also clears it).
The sequential next PC becomes
  inc = { c6 ? hi_p1_q : pc_w[29:6], pc_w[5:0] + 6'd1 },
  c6 = &pc_w[5:0],
so the loop is a 6-bit increment/AND plus a 2:1 mux instead of a
30-bit carry. npc_seq and the redirect D-mux keep their current form,
npc_seq stays (* syn_keep *), and bits [29:18] still use & ~pt_eff.
When hi_p1_q is stale (hi_stale_q & c6 & ~pt_eff, all from flops),
raise a new flop-sourced `carry_wait` from if_stage. hazard_unit treats
it exactly like !imem_ready: it goes into stall_if and into flush_id's
(redirect | load_use | imem_stall) term. The PC holds for one cycle and
the slot is killed and refetched, with hi_p1_q then valid. Redirect
still overrides the PC hold. Cost: one bubble only when a redirect or a
predicted-taken target lands on the last word of a 64-word block and
then falls through. By trace estimate that is under ~0.2% of cycles.
ID's pc4 must NOT share the IF `inc` any more (inc is wrong while
carry_wait is up), so keep ID's own `in.pc + 32'd4`. It feeds only ID/EX
flops (pc4, pre_result, alt_pc) and is flop-sourced from pc_w, so it is
not in any loop. pred_off (tgt18 - pc_w) is unchanged.

(B) Flat one-hot load forward. In EX, from the AGU low bits jalr_sum[1:0]
(the first bits of the carry chain, early) and ctrl.mem_width/mem_sext/
mem_to_reg, register into EX/MEM a small set of one-hot extract selects
for the MEM->ID forward value:
  b_sel[3:0]  : source byte lane for result bits [7:0] (loads only)
  h_hi        : bits [15:8] come from rdata[31:24] (LH/LHU at offset 2)
  h_lo        : bits [15:8] come from rdata[15:8]  (LH/LHU at 0 or LW)
  w_hi        : bits [31:16] come from rdata[31:16] (LW)
  s_sel[3:0]  : pre-masked with mem_sext, the one rdata bit (7/15/23/31)
                that is the fill sign for LB/LH at that offset
  f8, f16     : fill bits [15:8] / [31:16] with the sign
  alu         : !mem_to_reg (ALU result forward)
All of these are cleared by the existing div_stall/flush bubble logic
wherever ctrl.mem_read is cleared. mem_stage then computes
  sign    = |(s_sel & {rdata[31], rdata[23], rdata[15], rdata[7]})
  fwd_val = per-bit AND-OR of the selected rdata bits, sign and
            alu_result
so the BSRAM output passes one AND-OR level plus the sign OR, not the
shift mux, the width case and mem_to_reg. Keep `fwd_val` as a
(* syn_keep *) net so Gowin does not re-merge it into the rs2_res/op_b
muxes and grow a shared cone (r6s1). The MEM/WB read_data (regfile
write, RVFI) keeps the existing load_data extraction, so the WB path
and RVFI are unchanged. Only the ID forward value is rebuilt. Add no
new consumer on mem_fwd_val (r8s0 lesson).

Cycles: B changes none. A adds under 0.2% by trace estimate.
Fmax: A removes about 2 LUT levels / the upper carry from the logged
r9s2 critical loop. B removes about 2-3 LUT levels from the dmem ->
ID/EX family. Neither touches the EX bypass -> ALU/redirect cones, so
those two tied families bound the result. The expected gain is only
what those families leave, and it may be zero if they already sit at
~15.1 ns on option 1.

Implementation discipline (lessons r5s0 / r10s0 / r11s*): time A alone
and B alone on placement option 1 (the scored one) before combining.
Keep only cuts that do not lower option-1 Fmax. Report the option-1
top-10 endpoints for each build in implementation_notes.md. Check in
the netlist that inc[29:6] is a mux of hi_p1_q/pc_w and not a
re-inferred 30-bit adder, and that hi_p1_q's adder is not merged with
ID's pc4 adder in a way that puts it back in the loop. If needed, give
hi_p1_q a (* syn_preserve *) and make ID pc4 a separate kept net.

title: Posted-store dmem port: a store that sees dmem_ready=0 retires anyway while the existing mem_addr/write_data port flops keep presenting it until accepted
motivation:
The timed CoreMark region is 2.92M instructions in 4,215,892 cycles (CPI 1.444)
on r9s2. With imem_ready high 100/128 of cycles, the fetch floor is about
2.92M/0.781 = 3.74M cycles, so ~0.48M cycles are back-end losses. The largest
one is dmem backpressure: bench_stall_gen drives dmem_ready from a free-running
xorshift that does not depend on requests, and today any LOAD or STORE in MEM
that sees dmem_ready=0 freezes IF, ID/EX and EX/MEM (dmem_stall) for
~0.28 cycles on average (sum of 0.22^k). Every frozen cycle also wastes a
78%-likely imem-ready fetch slot, so these cycles add directly to the total.
For a STORE the freeze is not needed: nothing in the pipeline consumes a
store's result. The only requirement is that the write reaches memory before
any later memory access and before the program ends. Lessons r10s2, r11s0 and
r11s2 show that Fmax-only rewiring of r9s2's tied EX families lands in the
placement-noise band. This change removes cycles without adding any
logic to those families (EX bypass -> ALU -> alu_result, bypass -> compare ->
redirect -> pc_w/flush_id, dmem -> load extract -> op_b). It is a
structural change to the MEM stage's retirement rule, not to EX.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Let a STORE leave MEM on a cycle with dmem_ready=0. The dmem port
flops (EX/MEM.mem_addr, write_data, plus a new 2-bit width and 1-bit
"store" flop) stop loading and keep driving the posted write
until the bus accepts it. The rest of EX/MEM, MEM/WB, ID/EX and PC advance.

Keeping dmem_addr a bare flop is essential. The bench's 2048x32 async-read
dmem only maps to 4 BSRAMs because Gowin absorbs the core's mem_addr
flop into the BSRAM address register. So there must be NO mux between
that flop and io_dmemAddr: the posted store lives in the same flop, which
gets a separate clock enable. Nothing is added after the flop.

State: pend_q (1 flop) = the port flops hold a retired store that the bus
has not accepted yet. port_st = (EX/MEM store && !misalign) || pend_q (flops only).

Rules (all inputs are flops: dmem_ready, EX/MEM ctrl, pend_q, and the
ID/EX ctrl kill bits):
  1. dmem_stall (freeze everything exactly like today, lockstep kept, so the
     pre-decoded fwd1_ex/fwd2_ex bits stay exact) =
       !dmem_ready && ( EX/MEM is a LOAD
                      || (port_st && id_ex_needs_port) )
     where id_ex_needs_port = ID/EX.ctrl.mem_read | ctrl.mem_write |
     is_ebreak (a registered ID/EX bit). A memory op may not enter MEM while
     the port still holds an unaccepted store, so a later LOAD never overtakes
     the store and never needs a store-to-load forward. EBREAK waits so the
     harness never stops with a UART/stop-marker write still pending.
     FENCE can also be added to this set for strictness.
  2. A STORE in MEM with !dmem_ready and no port-needing op in EX: no
     stall. It retires into MEM/WB (RVFI reports mem_addr/wmask/wdata
     now, as before), and pend_q <= 1.
  3. pend_q && dmem_ready -> the write is accepted this cycle, pend_q <= 0.
  4. Port-flop CE: load (mem_addr, write_data, st_width_q, st_q) when
     !dmem_stall && !(port_st && !dmem_ready). Everything else in EX/MEM
     keeps CE = !dmem_stall. mem_addr, write_data and the width flop are
     don't-care for the non-memory ops that pass through MEM while pend_q
     is set (mem_misalign and the masks are gated by mem_op). load_data and
     fwd_val are only used when EX/MEM.mem_to_reg is set, which cannot
     happen while pend_q is set.
  5. dmem_wen = port_st ? mask(st_width_q, mem_addr[1:0]) : 0. wdata
     replication uses st_width_q. dmem_ren keeps using EX/MEM.mem_read.
     The MEM/WB RVFI mask/wdata fields keep using the EX/MEM occupant
     when it is the store itself (a store in MEM always has the port
     flops loaded with its own values, by rule 1).
Expected cycle effect: every store stall that is not immediately followed
by another memory op or EBREAK in EX disappears. Prologue store bursts
(sw ra; sw s0; ...) still stall as today. With ~6% of cycles lost to dmem
stalls in total and stores making up roughly a quarter to a third of the
dynamic memory ops, the expected saving is ~1.5-2.5% of cycles at
unchanged Fmax. The new logic is a few LUTs on flop-sourced
stall terms plus ~4 flops: pend_q, st_q, st_width_q and an ID/EX is_ebreak
bit.

Timing check the implementer must report: rule 1 makes dmem_stall
one LUT deeper, and dmem_stall gates flush_id and the EX/MEM, ID/EX and
pc_w enables. It is flop-sourced and must stay far earlier than redirect.
Confirm on the option-1 report that no top-10 path gains a dmem_stall
leg. Also confirm in the netlist that the 4 dmem BSRAMs are still
inferred with mem_addr absorbed. If they are not, the mem_addr CE
split is wrong: instead, hold mem_addr's CE equal to the port CE and
duplicate nothing after it.

Every existing consumer of dmem_stall (stall_if, stall_id, flush_id gating, stall_ex_mem, hold_mem_wb) is unchanged. Output port_hold = port_st && !dmem_ready for the port-flop CE.

Add pend_q (set when a non-misaligned STORE in MEM retires with !dmem_ready and there is no dmem_stall; cleared when dmem_ready). dmem_wen/wdata_rep use st_q/st_width_q with mem_addr (port flops) plus pend_q. dmem_ren stays EX/MEM.mem_read && !misalign. Register an is_ebreak bit (instr == 32'h00100073, cleared by the kill-bit flush like mem_read/mem_write) into ID/EX so hazard_unit can hold EBREAK in EX until a posted store is accepted.
Add id_ex_t.is_ebreak and the ex_mem_t port fields (st_q, st_width).
Wire pend_q/port_st from mem_stage, ID/EX mem_read|mem_write|is_ebreak and port_hold between hazard_unit, ex_stage and mem_stage. The RVFI mapping is unchanged.

cocotb: with dmem_ready held low for N cycles after a SW, the following ALU ops keep retiring, a LW to the same word placed 1 and 3 instructions later reads the new value, back-to-back SWs both land in order, and a UART write before EBREAK is accepted before EBREAK retires.

lesson: - 2026-09-30 hyp-20260930-002-r12s1 (regression, -2.74%): A posted-store dmem port (a STORE seeing dmem_ready=0 retires while separately enabled mem_addr/write_data/st/st_width flops keep driving it, and only a LOAD in MEM or a LOAD/STORE/EBREAK in EX behind the pending write still freezes the pipeline) was clean in every respect (4 dmem BSRAMs kept with mem_addr absorbed, formal and cosim pass, no dmem_stall leg in the option-0 top 10), but 244.85 at the scored 102.4 MHz median implies about 4.18M cycles, only -0.8% vs r9s2's 4,215,892 and half the 1.5-2.5% estimate (probably because many CoreMark stores sit next to another memory op, which still waits), while +46 LUTs alone moved the median from 106.1 to 102.4 MHz (option 0 98.2 vs 101.5) with the same redirect/ALU families on top; so keeping new logic off the critical families does not protect r9s2's high Fmax sample, and a cycle-only change here must cut well over 4% of cycles, measured in cosim before synthesis, to beat that noise (the formal wrapper ties dmem_ready=1, so only cosim and cocotb exercise a posted-store path).

title: Carry-free look-ahead BTB: registered sequential successor seq_q = pc_w+1 takes the incrementer off the pc_w and BTB-lookup loops
motivation:
r9s2 (champion, 251.74, 4,215,892 cycles, median 106.1 MHz) logged its
critical path as cpu/u_if/pc_w_1 -> cpu/u_if/pc_w_18 (10 cells, u_if
only). That path belongs to the look-ahead BTB: pc_w (high fanout: imem
BSRAM address, ID pc/pc4/pc_imm adders, pred_off) -> 30-bit +1 carry ->
kept npc_seq mux (pt_eff ? tgt18_q : inc) -> redirect D-mux -> pc_w.
The same carry also starts the BTB lookup loop: pc_w -> +1 -> npc_seq
-> RAM16 async read (addr npc_seq[3:0]) -> 8-bit tag compare against
npc_seq[11:4] -> pt_q/hit_q. So the predictor puts a carry chain from a
high-fanout flop at the head of both of its single-cycle loops. r11s0's
lesson says to shorten this IF loop before the EX families, because no
EX, ID or MEM work can lift Fmax past it.
More IPC from the predictor cannot clear the bar. r9s2's calibrated
trace model leaves only ~82K taken-branch bubbles (1.9% of cycles; 64
entries would recover only 17K of them) and 13.7K JALRs (0.33%). The
remaining predictor lever is the Fmax cost of the predictor's own
loops. r10s2/r11s0/r11s2 show that rewiring alone is noise, so the
change must remove real levels. This one removes the carry chain from
both IF loops.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Keep r9s2's predictor semantics: the 16-entry look-ahead BTB, the 8-bit
tag, the 18-bit target, the redir_q mask, pt folded into br_inv, the
flop-only ID pred_off check and replay, training from EX/MEM flops, and
JALR unpredicted. Change only how the sequential next PC is formed.

(1) Add a register seq_q[29:0] that holds pc_w + 1. The next fetch
    address comes from flops only:
      npc_seq = pt_eff ? {12'b0, tgt18_q} : seq_q    (kept, syn_keep)
      pc_w   <= redirect ? redirect_target[31:2] : npc_seq
    The pc_w CE is unchanged. The BTB lookup uses this carry-free
    npc_seq (RAM16 address npc_seq[3:0], tag compare npc_seq[11:4]).
(2) Pre-register the predicted target's successor. Next to tgt18_q, the
    lookup also registers tgtinc18_q <= rd[19:2] + 1 (18-bit carry after
    the RAM16 read; about as deep as the existing 8-bit tag compare ->
    pt_q path, with the same CE = !stall and no redirect term).
(3) seq_q's D input needs only one LUT after its own carry:
      alt_seq = seq_bad_q ? pc4_id[31:2] : {12'b0, tgtinc18_q}  (kept)
      use_alt = seq_bad_q | pt_eff                              (flops)
      seq_q  <= redirect_s ? e_inc : use_alt ? alt_seq : seq_q + 30'd1
    redirect_s is a third (* syn_keep *) copy of the redirect OR (like
    redirect_d/redirect_e), so the 30 new mux loads are not on the PC
    or flush_id copies. Write seq_q + 30'd1 as one explicit carry chain
    from the flop. The loop is flop -> carry -> 1 LUT5 -> D, one LUT
    shorter than today's pc_w loop, and seq_q fans out only to npc_seq,
    its own adder and this mux. seq_q CE = pc_w's CE | seq_bad_q.
(4) ID precomputes the word successor of every non-JALR redirect target,
    e_inc[29:0]. It is an unflushed ID/EX data field and is fully selected
    in ID, because replay/jfix/pt are all known there:
      replay -> pc4[31:2]
      jfix   -> pc_imm4[31:2]
      else   -> in.pt ? pc4[31:2] + 1 : pc_imm4[31:2]
    pc_imm4 = pc4 + imm is a new ID adder parallel to pc_imm, and
    pc4[31:2] + 1 comes from pc + 8, which is imm-free. EX exports
    in.e_inc unchanged (flop-only), so the redirect cone does not change.
(5) JALR (13.7K dynamic, all returns): do not compute its successor,
    because that needs a carry after jalr_sum on the bypassed rs1. On a
    JALR redirect (jalr_np && !jalr_bit1, a flop-sourced qualifier plus
    the existing redirect), set seq_bad_q for one cycle. hazard_unit
    treats a seq_bad_q cycle like an imem-stall slot: stall_if and
    flush_id (kill bits only), gated off on dmem/div stall like
    imem_stall. So pc_w holds on the JALR target, and seq_q is repaired
    from ID's existing pc + 4 adder (pc4_id, i.e. pc_w + 1). The repair
    is idempotent while pc_w holds. The fetch repeats next cycle.
    redir_q stays set through the bubble (redirect | stall & redir_q),
    so the first real fetch after the redirect is still unpredicted
    (liveness unchanged). cur_q's CE = !stall skips the bubble's
    garbage lookup. EX cannot redirect in the bubble cycle, because the
    JALR redirect flushed ID/EX (or, under dmem/div stall, the JALR is
    held and redirects again idempotently). Cost: 1 cycle per JALR,
    ~13.7K cycles (+0.33%).
(6) Keep every r9s2 timing rule: syn_keep on npc_seq and on the redirect
    copies, the fast_or | mul_or late DSP join untouched, and no new
    consumer on alu_result, mem_fwd_val, the rs1/rs2 bypass outputs or
    the fwd selects. Before building the rest, confirm in the netlist
    that npc_seq has no carry cell in its fan-in, and that Gowin did not
    fold pt_eff/seq_q into pc_w's CE (the r5s2 failure).

Expected: cycles ~4.230M (+0.33%). The ~18-bit carry ripple and the
high-fanout pc_w net leave the logged IF critical path and the BTB
lookup loop, so option 0 should rise from 101.5 toward the ~106 MHz EX
family limit. Options 1/2 gain only if their 11-cell worst paths
include this IF loop. Clearing the bar (263.3, ~111.4 MHz at 4.23M)
needs that. If they are EX-limited, expect roughly flat fitness. Report
all three options' worst paths and the cycle count, so the next round
knows whether IF still limits the median-setting option.

lesson: - 2026-09-30 hyp-20260930-003-r12s2 (regression, -8.07%): Taking the +1 carry out of r9s2's pc_w and BTB-lookup loops with a registered successor (seq_q = pc_w+1) needed a repair network that must be exact on every PC load: a 30-bit e_inc ID/EX field fed by two new ID adders (pc+imm+4, pc+8), a registered tgtinc18_q for predicted targets, a third kept redirect copy that drives 30 seq_q mux loads, and a one-cycle seq_bad bubble after each JALR that is ORed into both stall_if and flush_id; it scored 231.42, which at the planned ~4.23M cycles implies a median (10*Fmax/Mcycles) of ~97.9 MHz, 8 MHz below r9s2's 106.1 and about twice the 3-5 MHz noise of r10s2/r11s0/r11s2 (cycles would have to rise 8.8% to explain the loss at r9s2's Fmax); no cycle count or per-option timing was reported, but the likely cause is that a shadow register does not delete the carry, it moves the carry into repair glue, and that glue lands on the tied families that r9s2's single logged pc_w_1 -> pc_w_18 path hides (seq_bad sits on redirect -> flush_id -> ID/EX kill and on stall_if -> pc_w CE, the redirect cone gains loads, and ~80 new flops plus two 30-bit adders add area, where r12s1 lost ~3.7 MHz to +46 LUTs alone); so r11s0's "fix the IF loop first" is necessary but not sufficient, and an IF cut on r9s2 pays only if it adds no stall/flush source, no redirect-cone load and little area, which rules out shadow-incrementer schemes like seq_q and r12s0's hi_p1_q/carry_wait (r12s0's log matches r9s2 exactly, 2681 LUT / 790 FF / same path, so it was never really built).

title: Flop-free IF next-PC split (18-bit carry chain + parallel upper carry-in, pt mask folded) and one-hot registered load-lane selects, zero new stall/flush/redirect loads
motivation:
r9s2 (251.74, 106.1 MHz median, 4,215,892 cycles) logs its option-1
critical path as cpu/u_if/pc_w_1 -> pc_w_18 (10 cells, u_if only): the
carry of the 30-bit pc_w + 1 incrementer ripples from bit 1 into bit 18,
then goes through the kept npc_seq mask (inc[29:18] & ~pt_eff) and the
redirect D-mux into pc_w. r11s0 showed that no EX/ID/MEM change can lift
Fmax past that path, and r12s2/r12s0 showed that shadow incrementers
(seq_q, hi_p1_q + carry_wait) fail because their repair glue adds a
stall/flush source, redirect-cone loads and ~80 flops. The other family
named by r10s2/r11s2/r6s1 that does not pass through the EX/MEM bypass
is dmem BSRAM -> load extract (4:1 byte shift, then width/sign case)
-> fwd_val -> rs2_res -> op_b. Both can be shortened with purely
combinational restructuring that adds no flops on IF, no stall, no
flush term and no load on redirect_d/redirect_e.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
(A) IF next-PC, no new state. Replace `inc = pc_w + 1` (30-bit) with
two independent pieces: inc_lo[17:0] = pc_w[17:0] + 1 written as an
explicit kept carry-chain add (so Gowin maps it to ALU cells and cannot
rebuild it as a LUT tree, cf. r7s0's compare lesson), and the upper
half npc_seq[29:18] computed directly as
`(pc_w[29:18] + {11'b0, c18}) & ~pt_eff` where c18 = &pc_w[17:0] is a
kept 18-input AND built as a 2-level LUT4 tree (5 LUT4 + 1 LUT4) that
starts from pc_w flops in parallel with the low chain, so bit 18..29
see ~3 LUT levels instead of an 18-bit ripple. The pt_eff mask on the
upper half is folded into the same kept LUT (inputs pc_w[i], carry-in
term, pt_eff) instead of a separate AND after the increment.
npc_seq stays kept (BTB lookup reads npc_seq[11:0]; bit 11 is inside
the fast low chain). pc_w D-mux / CE, redir_q, pt_q, tgt18_q, the
lookup and the ID pred_off check are unchanged, so the architectural
PC sequence, BTB behavior and cycle count (4,215,892) are identical.
(B) Load extract as one AND-OR level. In EX, register one-hot
load-lane selects next to EX/MEM.mem_addr from jalr_sum[1:0] and the
decoded width/sext (ld_w, ld_b[3:0], ld_h[1:0], ld_sx8, ld_sx16,
ld_zx), and also a registered copy of mem_to_reg reserved for the
load extract. mem_stage then forms load_data per output bit as a
single flat AND-OR of dmem_rdata bytes/halves and the fill bit
(fill = sx8 & selected byte[7] | sx16 & selected half[15]), with no
4:1 shift followed by a separate width case. fwd_val and the ID rs2_res
/ op_b muxes are untouched (per r8s0/r9s0, no new consumer is hung
on the load-forward net and the DSP operand path is not touched).
Build and time (A) alone first on place option 1 (the scored median;
options 1 and 2 always match), then (A)+(B); keep (B) only if option 1
does not drop. Report per-option top-10 paths for each build.
Correctness: both parts are pure logic rewrites; formal (ALTOPS) and
cosim must match r9s2 exactly, and the cycle count must equal
4,215,892.

lesson: - 2026-09-30 hyp-20260930-001-r13s0 (regression, -7.07%): A purely combinational IF/MEM rewrite that met r12s2's conditions (no new IF state, stall, flush or redirect-cone load) still scored 233.93, an implied median (10*Fmax/Mcycles) of ~98.6 MHz at r9s2's unchanged 4,215,892 cycles vs 106.1, most likely because neither part removed a logic level on its target's worst bit while both added area: (A) split the `pc_w + 1` incrementer exactly at bit 18, the endpoint of r9s2's logged pc_w_1 -> pc_w_18 path, so the worst endpoint only moves to bit 17 (the kept inc_lo ripple from bit 1, then the `pt_eff ? tgt18_q` mux and the redirect D-mux), one carry cell shorter, and only bits 18-29 got the new kept c18/hi_p lookahead LUTs; (B)'s flat AND-OR still builds the load_data[31:8] sign fill from an 8-input `fb & {rd[31], rd[23], rd[15], rd[7]}` select (2 LUT4 levels) before the final OR, about the same depth as the 4:1 shift + sext case it replaced, and adds 13 EX/MEM ld flops; the planned A-alone option-1 build that would have separated the two parts was not reported; so to cut a logged carry path, split where the longest remaining piece is well shorter than the logged one (e.g., a carry-select above ~bit 9, not at the endpoint bit), and before building a flatten, count LUT4 levels on its worst output bit (such as the sign-fill fanout), not on a typical bit.

title: Bypass-at-D on r9s2 with the load leg one LUT before the flop: EX reads bare ID/EX flops, the EX result joins the operand D input in the last LUT
motivation:
r9s2 (251.74, 106.1 MHz median, 4,215,892 cycles) is limited by tied families
that all start at the EX/MEM -> EX bypass mux: fwd1_ex -> ALU -> alu_result,
fwd1_ex -> branch compare -> redirect -> pc_w / flush_id, the rs1 bypass ->
AGU -> dmem address, plus dmem -> load extract -> mem_fwd_val -> rs2_res -> op_b.
Lessons r10s2, r11s0, r11s2 and r12s1 show that rewiring, replicating or
trimming area moves Fmax only inside a 3-5 MHz placement-noise band. To clear
the 4.6% bar at unchanged cycles (~111 MHz) a change must remove real logic
levels from all of these families at once. r6s1 showed that moving the bypass
mux from EX's input to the ID/EX D side removes one level from every EX path
(option 0 went from 98.7 to 103.1 MHz on r4s0). It gained only 0.8% on the
median because the load-forward path then became the limit: dmem -> extract
-> mem_fwd_val -> rs2_res -> fwd_ex mux -> op_b mux -> flop, with Gowin also
sharing logic across the three D muxes. The r6s1 lesson names the fix: give
the load leg slack before adding the ex_out leg. This hypothesis makes both
changes together, with a fixed LUT order, on the r9s2 base.

the load leg slack before adding the ex_out leg. This hypothesis makes both
changes together, with a fixed LUT order, on the r9s2 base.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Restructure where operands are resolved, so every EX consumer (ALU, DSP,
shifter, branch compare, JALR/AGU adder, store data) reads bare ID/EX flops
and the bypass is paid on the D side, where it merges into LUTs that already
exist.

(1) Bypass-at-D (from r6s1). Delete the EX input muxes (rs1/rs2/alu_b =
fwd ? reg_q.alu_result : ...) and div_rs1_q/div_rs2_q. ID/EX.rs1_val,
rs2_val and op_b load
    rs1_D = fwd1_ex ? ex_out : rest1
    rs2_D = fwd2_ex ? ex_out : rest2
    opb_D = fwdb_ex ? ex_out : restb
where ex_out = fast_or | mul_or (the EX-stage result, unregistered).
The final LUT must be the only LUT after the ALU: write it as
fwd ? (fast_or | mul_or) : rest, a single LUT4 per bit that takes the kept
fast_or/mul_or nets directly, so the ALU loop is flop -> ALU -> fast_or -> 1
LUT -> flop. Today it is flop -> bypass mux -> ALU -> fast_or -> out -> flop,
so this removes one level from the ALU loop. The redirect, AGU and DSP paths
also each lose the bypass level. fwd*_ex are already computed in ID
(forward_unit, same-cycle ex_wb_kill, which now comes from flop-only
jalr_bit1). ID/EX captures only when EX/MEM also advances (stall_id covers
every dmem/div stall), so a held DIV keeps its resolved operands in ID/EX.
That is why div_rs*_q can be dropped. EX/MEM.rs1_val/rs2_val/write_data then
read the ID/EX flops directly.

(2) Load leg one LUT before the flop, with the ALU leg last. Split the
MEM-stage forward:
    rest1 = ld1 ? load_data : oth1,  oth1 = fwd1_mem ? ex_mem.alu_result : rs1_data
    restb = ldb ? load_data : othb,  othb = alu_src ? imm : (fwd2_mem ? ex_mem.alu_result : rs2_data)
with ld1 = fwd1_mem & ex_mem.mem_to_reg and ldb = fwd2_mem & mem_to_reg &
!alu_src. These selects come from the raw imem word against EX/MEM flops and
arrive early, beside the BSRAM clock-to-out. mem_fwd_val loses its
mem_to_reg mux: ALU values now come straight from the EX/MEM flop. Load
extraction uses registered one-hot lane selects, computed in EX from
jalr_sum[1:0] (the AGU's low bits come off the carry chain first) and
mem_width/mem_sext, and stored in EX/MEM: b0..b3, h0/h1, w, sx. Each
load_data bit is then a flat AND-OR of at most 4 candidates plus a fill bit.
The load path becomes BSRAM -> ~2-level extract -> rest LUT -> final LUT ->
flop. Today it is extract -> mem_fwd_val -> rs2_res -> op_b, and in r6s1 it
also passed through fwd_ex. The branch compare, JALR target and misalign
checks read the bare flops, and nothing else changes in the redirect cone.
Put (* syn_keep *) on rest1/rest2/restb, oth*, and load_data, so Gowin
cannot rebuild opb_D as alu_src ? imm : rs2_D (the r6s1 92.1 MHz first
build).

(3) IF loop, spending the level that (1) frees on redirect. r9s2's logged
top path is pc_w_1 -> pc_w_18: the +1 carry, then the kept npc_seq LUT, then
the redirect D-mux LUT. After (1), redirect arrives one level earlier (no
bypass mux in front of the compare). So re-order the pc_w D input to
    pc_D = sel_inc ? inc : other
    sel_inc = !redirect & !pt_eff
    other = redirect ? redirect_target : (bits [17:0]: tgt18_q, bits [29:18]: 0)
with sel_inc and other kept. The carry output then passes one LUT instead of
two, and redirect passes two, the same depth it has today from the bypass
mux. Keep npc_seq (kept) only for the BTB lookup index/tag and the ID
pred_off, unchanged. CE stays redirect_ce | !stall, and redirect gains no
new flop loads (sel_inc/other are 60 LUT loads, replacing the 30 D-mux
loads). Build and time (3) only after (1)+(2). Keep it only if option 1
improves.

Cycles are unchanged: forwarding sources, stall/flush and redirect timing
are the same, so the ~4.216M cycles hold. The expected result: every EX
family and the load family lose 1-2 LUT levels (~0.6-1.0 ns of ~9.4 ns),
and the IF loop loses one LUT, for ~111-115 MHz.

Verification requirements, from the lessons: pick and check every cut on the

a cocotb directed test that covers a DIV followed by a dependent op, a
load-use pair, an I-2 load consumer with LB/LH/LBU/LHU at every byte offset,
and a store whose data comes from the immediately preceding ALU op.

title: Carry-free look-ahead BTB: flop-indexed lookup and a one-level predicted-PC D mux
motivation:
r9s2's scored critical path (log.jsonl) is the predictor's own IF loop:
cpu/u_if/pc_w_1 -> pc_w_18 (10 cells, u_if only). The look-ahead BTB put
two things on the pc_w loop that r4s0 did not have: the kept npc_seq mux
(pt_eff ? tgt18_q : inc, plus inc & ~pt_eff for bits 29:18) sits as its
own LUT level between the +1 carry and the redirect D mux, and pt_eff is
itself a gate (pt_q & ~redir_q) in front of those 30 mux selects. The
lookup path is even longer: pc_w -> +1 carry up to bit 11 -> npc_seq mux
-> RAM16 async read (index npc_seq[3:0]) -> 8-bit tag compare against
npc_seq[11:4] -> pt_q/hit_q. Both paths exist only because of the
predictor, and neither adds a single predicted branch.
The remaining predictor cycle headroom is small (trace model: 82K of
4.216M cycles are branch bubbles; JALR 13.7K, post-redirect 6.6K,
capacity ~17K), so the predictor slot's best lever is to stop the
predictor from costing Fmax, not to predict more. Lessons r10s2/r11s0/
r11s2 say only a real logic-level cut beats placement noise; this change
removes one LUT level from the pc_w loop and the whole 12-bit carry from
the lookup path without adding any net to the EX redirect cone, flush_id,
the EX bypass loops or the load-forward net.
