hypothesis.hypothesis:
Keep r9s2's predictor semantics exactly (16 entries, 8-bit tag, 18-bit
zero-extended word target, 2-bit counter, redir_q mask, ID pred_off
check/replay, EX/MEM-flop training). Change only how IF forms the next PC
and the look-ahead index/tag:

1. Registered select. Add a flop pte_q that equals pt_eff for the current
   cycle: pte_q <= reset ? 0 : (!stall ? (l_hit & rd[1]) : pt_q) &
   ~(redirect | (stall & redir_q)). Its D uses the same inputs as pt_q and
   redir_q today (one extra load on redirect, a flop D, not the PC CE).
   pt_eff := pte_q (keep pt_q/redir_q for out.pt/out.hit semantics or
   derive them identically).
2. One-level PC D mux. pc_w's D is built per bit directly from flops and
   the carry: bits [17:0]: redirect ? rt : (pte_q ? tgt18_q : inc);
   bits [29:18]: redirect ? rt : (inc & ~pte_q). Mark the per-bit D value
   (* syn_keep *) as pc_d so Gowin maps it as one LUT4/MUX2_LUT5 after the
   carry and cannot fold the pte_q leg into the CE (r5s2 lesson). The kept
   npc_seq net stays, but drives only the lookup (step 3) and not pc_w.
3. Carry-free lookup (exact, identical predictions). The RAM16 index
   becomes idx = pte_q ? tgt18_q[3:0] : (pc_w[3:0] + 1) (a 4-bit
   increment, no long carry). Entries store an adjusted tag: training
   writes tag = (pc[5:2] == 0) ? pc[13:6] - 1 : pc[13:6] (EX/MEM flops
   only, an 8-bit decrement off every critical family). Then the
   sequential reference is exactly pc_w[11:4] (flops): for a branch at
   B = P+1 with B[3:0] != 0, P[11:4] == B[11:4]; with B[3:0] == 0,
   P[11:4] == B[11:4] - 1, which is the stored tag. For the
   predicted-target leg the reference must apply the same adjust to the
   target, so register it one cycle early: when the lookup loads
   tgt18_q <= rd.tgt, also load tadj_q <= rd.tgt[11:4] - (rd.tgt[3:0] == 0)
   (an 8-bit decrement in parallel with the existing tag compare, from
   the RAM16 read to a flop). tref = pte_q ? tadj_q : pc_w[11:4] (flops
   only, one LUT, computed in parallel with the RAM read);
   l_hit = (rd.tag == tref). The first fetch after a redirect stays
   unpredicted (pte_q = 0 there), and the lookup in that cycle already
   uses the correct sequential index/tag of the redirect target.
   Fallback if tadj_q proves slow: drop it and guard the target leg with
   tgt18_q[3:0] != 0 (target-is-a-branch at a line start is rare).
   Training is unchanged apart from the tag adjust.
4. Nothing else moves: redirect/redirect_ce, flush_id, the ID pred_off
   check (it still reads tgt18_q and pc_w, both flops), EX, MEM and the
   regfile are untouched.

Expected effect: the scored pc_w loop loses the separate npc_seq LUT level
and the pt_eff gate (carry -> 1 LUT -> pc_w D), and the lookup path goes
from a 12-bit carry + mux + RAM16 + compare to flop -> 1-2 LUT index ->
RAM16 -> compare, so the IF family drops out of the tied top set.
With the exact tag-adjust variant cycles stay at 4,215,892 (identical
predictions; cosim cycle count must match r9s2 exactly, which is a cheap
correctness check of the adjust); the fallback guard costs well under
0.1%.
Area is roughly neutral (a 4-bit incrementer and 8 tref muxes replace
nothing on EX). The implementer must time options 1 and 2 (the scored
median) and report the top paths per option, and verify in the netlist
that pc_d is one LUT level after the carry.

lesson: - 2026-09-30 hyp-20260930-003-r13s2 (regression, -0.95%): The flop-indexed look-ahead BTB scored 249.34, which at r9s2's 4,215,892 cycles implies a median (10*Fmax/Mcycles) of ~105.1 MHz vs 106.1, inside the placement-noise band, because the build did not remove a level from the scored pc_w_1 -> pc_w_18 loop: step 2's one-level per-bit kept pc_d was not built, pc_d = redirect ? rt : npc still reads the syn_keep'd npc net, so the path is still carry -> kept npc LUT -> redirect LUT exactly as in r9s2, and registering pt_eff into pte_q most likely saved nothing, since `(pt_q & ~redir_q) ? tgt : inc` has only 4 inputs and already fits in one LUT4 with the mux, while the carry-free lookup (4-bit index increment plus adjusted tags B[11:4] - (B[3:0] == 0), an exact way to index and tag a look-ahead table from pc_w flops that can be reused) cut a path that was not the scored one; so before counting a gate as a LUT level, count the LUT4 inputs of the whole cone, and check that no syn_keep net sits between the levels you mean to merge, because a kept net forces its own level.

title: MULH* on the divider's registered handshake (product from quo_q/dvs_q flops) so the EX result join loses the mul_or level, plus an unkept one-LUT pc_d
motivation:
On r9s2 the scored option-1 paths are two tied loops: the IF loop
pc_w -> +1 carry -> kept npc_seq LUT -> redirect LUT -> pc_w (15.15 ns, 10
cells) and the EX loop EX/MEM alu_result -> bypass LUT -> DSP -> kept mul_or
LUT -> out LUT -> alu_result (r13s2's scored path, 14.75 ns, 5 cells). Seven
r9s2 derivatives that rewired or replicated nets without removing a level
landed in the 98-105 MHz noise band. The lessons say to remove a real LUT
level from each tied loop, and to check that no syn_keep net sits between the
levels to be merged (r13s2).
The DSP loop has a removable level. mul_or exists only because MULLO and MULHI
share the DSP output and need a 2-way select before the final OR. CoreMark's
timed region is almost entirely MUL (low): the matrix kernels. MULH/MULHU/
MULHSU are rare there, so they can go through the multi-cycle path the
divider already has.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
(A) EX loop. MULH, MULHU and MULHSU join the RS_DIV class and use the
existing divider handshake, like the ALTOPS divide. On div_start the raw
operands latch into quo_q/dvs_q, which already happens. Next cycle is fix_q:
quo_q <= product(quo_q, dvs_q, latched sign bits)[63:32], then done. A MULH*
therefore costs 2 stall cycles, and the RVFI rs1/rs2 latches (div_rs*_q) are
reused unchanged. The 33x33 DSP is now fed only by flops and ends at the quo_q
D mux, so it is completely off the bypass loop. MUL (low) keeps a
single-cycle combinational 32x32 low-half multiply on the bypassed a/alu_b,
with signedness irrelevant. The result join becomes one kept LUT per bit:
out = fast_or | (sel[RS_MULLO] & mul_lo). The kept mul_or level is deleted,
and a truncated 32-bit product may also map to a shallower DSP cascade than
the full 66-bit one. Under ALTOPS, the MULH* stand-ins
((a+b)^k / (a-b)^k) are applied in the fix cycle from the latched operands,
exactly as the ALTOPS divide already is.
(B) IF loop. Delete the syn_keep on npc_seq and register pt_eff as one flop,
pte_q (the same next-state as pt_q & ~redir_q). Then each pc_w D bit is a
single function of {redirect, redirect_target[i], pte_q, tgt18_q[i]/0,
inc[i]} with no kept net between the carry and the redirect mux: the late
carry goes into the last LUT4, or into the MUX2_LUT5 data leg. The BTB
lookup keeps its own unkept copy of the npc_seq index/tag.
Cycle cost is only the MULH* stalls, estimated below 0.3% of cycles. If
both loops each lose a level, option 1 should move from about 106 to about
111-113 MHz.

changes.description: Split the multiplier. mul_lo = a*b is a single-cycle 32-bit truncated product. MULH/MULHU/MULHSU use the divider FSM: start latches the raw operands and sign flags (a_signed/b_signed), fix_q computes the 33x33 product of quo_q/dvs_q into quo_q[63:32 slice], and done. The ALTOPS stand-ins move into the fix cycle next to the ALTOPS divide. mul_or is deleted; out = fast_or | (sel[RS_MULLO] & mul_lo), with fast_or kept.
Decode MULH/MULHU/MULHSU into alu_sel[RS_DIV] (RS_MULHI is retired or left permanently zero). Keep a_signed/b_signed registered for the latch at start.
is_div also covers MULH*: the same div_stall/div_start/div_ack and div_rs*_q latches. No other change.

Remove syn_keep from npc_seq and add pte_q (reset 0, CE = !stall, D = next-cycle pt & ~next redir, the same value as pt_q & ~redir_q). title: Early dmem slot for loads: a load whose base is already in the regfile gets its access in EX (address from an ID-stage AGU), removing its load-use bubble and giving it a second try in MEM
motivation:
Every Fmax-only change on r9s2 since round 10 has landed inside the
3-5 MHz placement-noise band (r10s2, r11s0, r11s2, r12s1, r13s0-s2), so
the 4.6% bar has to come mostly from cycles, and it has to come from
logic that does not touch the tied families (fwd1_ex -> ALU ->
alu_result, fwd1_ex -> redirect -> pc_w, pc_w +1 loop, dmem -> load
extract -> op_b).
r5s1's CPI budget (CPI ~1.5) is: imem-not-ready ~0.28-0.31 (fixed by
the 22% xorshift, CPI floor 1/0.78 = 1.28), taken-redirect ~0.12 (now
mostly removed by the BTB), dmem stalls ~0.08, load-use ~0.06-0.10.
After the BTB, the two back-end stalls (load-use and dmem) are each
about 5% of cycles, and both come from the same structure: the single
dmem port is only ever used in MEM, one cycle after the address is
known, and the only chance a load gets is the one MEM cycle, whose
ready bit is an independent 78% roll. The dmem port sits idle in about
70% of cycles (no mem op in MEM), so a load can be given its access one
stage earlier whenever its address is available in ID and the port is
free in its EX cycle.
Front-end banking (the IQ, tried 4 times) always put a mux in front of
decode and lost Fmax; this idea adds nothing in front of decode and
nothing on the redirect cone or the pc_w loop.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a second, earlier dmem slot for loads ("early try"), keeping the
existing MEM-stage access as the fallback. No new stall or flush source
and no new redirect load. Cycle behaviour for every other instruction is
unchanged.

(1) ID-stage AGU on the raw regfile read. reg_file exposes a raw read
port rs1_raw = regs[rs1_addr] (no write-first mux). ID computes
id_agu = rs1_raw + imm (imm_gen I-type, only [12:0] matter for the
BSRAM address; keep full width for RVFI/OOB but the carry chain is
short). A LOAD in ID is early-eligible (ID/EX data field early_q,
registered, NOT a new kill bit) iff: dec_mem_read, rs1 is not the ID/EX
occupant's rd with reg_write set (conservative compare WITHOUT
ex_wb_kill, so no EX-late signal reaches early_q), not the EX/MEM occupant's
(reuse fwd1_mem), not the regfile write this cycle (wb_w_en &&
wb_w_addr == rs1), and the access is aligned (mem_width vs
(rs1_raw[1:0] + imm[1:0])). Register the byte offset id_agu[1:0] as
early_off. No forward leg ever feeds id_agu, so no load-data or ALU
bypass net gets a new consumer.

(2) One dmem address register with a flop-decided owner. Replace the
EX/MEM.mem_addr -> io_dmemAddr connection with dmem_addr_q (the flop
Gowin absorbs into the dmem BSRAM address register, as mem_addr is
today): on dmem_stall hold; else if the ID/EX occupant will enter
EX/MEM as a live mem op (ctrl.mem_read|mem_write && !early_hit) load
jalr_sum (the EX AGU, today's value); else load id_agu (the next
load's early address; don't-care when no load is behind). EX/MEM.mem_addr
stays for RVFI and the misalign check. io_dmemAddr must stay a bare
flop output: test/cosim/main.cpp computes io_dmemRData from
io_dmemAddr BEFORE eval(), so a combinational address would read stale
data. Pointer chasing also gains: a load whose base is the early-hit
load's rd is ineligible itself but no longer bubbles, and uses the EX
AGU through the existing fwd1_ex bypass. The only new inputs of the
address D mux are flop bits and dmem_ready.

(3) Early try in EX. early_try = ID/EX.early_q && ID/EX.ctrl.mem_read
(existing kill bit) && !ex_mem_mem_op (port free: MEM has no mem op,
so every older store has already written — ordering is preserved and
dmem_stall and early_try are mutually exclusive). io_dmemREn =
MEM-stage ren | early_try; io_dmemWEn stays MEM-stage only.
early_hit = early_try && io_dmemReady.
 - Data: ID sets a new one-hot class RS_LD (instead of RS_ADD) for
   early-eligible loads. alu.sv builds ld_or = sel[RS_LD] & extract(
   io_dmemRData, early_off, width, sext) as a third kept partial OR,
   out = fast_or | mul_or | ld_or (still one LUT4 after the DSP, per
   r5s0's rule; nothing is added to fast_or).
 - Control: EX/MEM.ctrl.mem_read and mem_to_reg load
   `x && !early_hit`, so an early-hit load leaves EX as an ALU-like
   result (MEM does not access again; mem_fwd_val and WB take
   alu_result). On a miss the load is exactly today's load (garbage
   alu_result is never read because mem_to_reg stays 1).
 - Load-use: hazard_unit's load_use_hazard gains `&& !early_hit`
   (early_hit is flop bits AND the ready input, so the stall_if ->
   pc_w CE path grows by at most one LUT input). The consumer then
   enters ID/EX with its already-computed fwd1_ex/fwd2_ex and reads
   the loaded value through the existing EX/MEM.alu_result bypass —
   no new forward leg in ID or EX.
 - RVFI: carry the early rdata/rmask/aligned addr in EX/MEM fields
   that mem_stage selects for MEM/WB when the op was early (RVFI-only,
   pruned in synthesis).

Expected effect: an early-eligible load with a consumer right behind
loses its 1-cycle bubble (plus the ~0.28 refetch roll) with p = 0.78,
and an early-eligible load that misses in EX still gets its normal
MEM try, so its dmem-stall probability falls from 0.22 to ~0.05.
If ~60% of loads are eligible (base not produced by I-1/I-2), that is
~0.035 CPI of load-use plus ~0.025 CPI of dmem stall, about 4% of
cycles, at ~+60 LUTs and ~+40 FFs with no logic added to the ALU
loop depth, the redirect cone or the IF loop.

Implementation order (lessons r12s1/r10s1/r13s1):
 a) Build (1)-(3), run cosim and report the CoreMark cycle count vs
    r9s2's 4,215,892 BEFORE synthesis; also count how many loads were
    early-eligible and how many early_hit. If cycles fall < 3%, stop

 b) `make timing` and report option 1's top 10 paths; confirm the
    dmem address is still absorbed into the BSRAM (4 BSRAMs, no fabric
    address flops), that ld_or/out is one LUT after mul_or, and that
    the new paths (imem -> LUTRAM -> id_agu[12:0] -> dmem_addr_q D;
    dmem -> extract -> ld_or -> alu_result D) are not in the top 10.

title: Finish the carry-free look-ahead BTB: registered pte_q and one MUX2_LUT5 pc_d per bit, no kept npc net in the pc_w loop
motivation:
r9s2's scored critical path in log.jsonl is the predictor's own IF loop
(cpu/u_if/pc_w_1 -> pc_w_18, 10 cells, u_if only). The look-ahead BTB
added one LUT level to that loop compared with the BTB-less r4s0:
pc_w -> +1 carry -> kept npc_seq LUT (pt_q & ~redir_q ? tgt18_q : inc)
-> redirect D LUT -> pc_w. r13s2 was meant to remove it, but its step 2
(one-level pc_d) was never built: pc_d still read the syn_keep'd npc net,
so the loop kept both LUT levels, and only the carry-free lookup (step 3)
landed. r13s2 still scored 105.1 MHz with the ALU loop on top, so the
lookup cut alone is Fmax-neutral and harmless; the loop cut was never
measured.
The predictor's cycle headroom is small (trace model: 82K of 4.216M
cycles are control bubbles; JALR 13.7K = 0.33%, post-redirect 6.6K,
capacity ~17K), so no direction/target improvement can reach the 4.6%
bar. The only predictor lever left is to remove the Fmax the predictor
costs on the loops it shares with the redirect family.

Keep r9s2's predictor semantics bit-exact (16 entries, 8-bit tag, 18-bit
zero-extended word target, 2-bit counter, redir_q liveness mask, ID
pred_off check/replay, EX/MEM-flop training, JALR untrained). Cosim cycle
count must equal r9s2's 4,215,892 exactly; that is the correctness check.

(1) Registered select pte_q == pt_eff. pte_q <= reset ? 0 :

    Use a plain flop (no syn_keep / CE games) with the same enable as

    Per bit i:
      bits [17:0] : pc_d[i] = redirect ? rt[i] : (pte_q ? tgt18_q[i] : inc[i])
      bits [29:18]: pc_d[i] = redirect ? rt[i] : (inc[i] & ~pte_q)

    the carry and the redirect select (r13s2 lesson). CE stays
    redirect_ce | !stall exactly as today. Count the inputs: inner term
    is 3 inputs (pte_q, tgt18_q[i], inc[i]) + redirect + rt[i] = 5, one
    LUT5 = LUT4 + in-slice MUX2, with no routing hop between them.
    If Gowin still inserts a routed LUT between inc and the redirect mux
    (check the netlist: pc_w D must be LUT4 -> MUX2_LUT5 -> DFFE),
    fall back to instantiating the per-bit LUT4 + MUX2_LUT5 Gowin
    primitives under `ifndef VERILATOR` with the generic RTL as the
    Verilator/formal model.

    has no long carry and the npc net is no longer needed at all;
    delete npc_seq if nothing else reads it.

    pred_off check, MEM, regfile untouched. No new stall or flush source,
    no new ID/EX field.

depth, one routed LUT hop shorter than r9s2/r13s2), and the
fwd1_ex -> compare -> redirect -> pc_w family also ends on a MUX2 select

leaves the tied set; the ALU loop (r13s2's scored 5-cell alu_result
loop) then limits, so the likely result is +0..+4%, and the change
wins only if the shorter PC endpoints let placement relieve the ALU
loop. The implementer must report option-1 top-10 paths, the pc_w D
netlist structure, and the cosim cycle count.

title: DSP off the EX bypass loop: MUL* read bare ID/EX flops, replay a MUL that needs the EX/MEM bypass
motivation:
On r9s2 the clock is set by tied EX families that all start at the
EX/MEM alu_result flop and the registered fwd*_ex selects. The slowest
member is the multiplier loop: EX/MEM.alu_result -> fwd1_ex/fwd2_ex 2:1
bypass LUT -> 33x33 DSP (combinational) -> mul_or -> out ->
EX/MEM.alu_result. r4s0 made the DSP join last; nothing since has taken
the bypass LUT and its routing out of the DSP input. Every earlier try at
that (r1s1 multi-cycle MUL, r4s1 MUL in MEM, r8s0/r9s0 ID-loaded DSP
operand flops, r14s0 MULH on the divider handshake) added cycles, glue,
or new operand flops that Gowin absorbed into the DSP input registers.
r9s0's lesson named that absorption as the cause: dedicated flops that
feed only the DSP get pulled into its fixed-column input register.
This plan adds no new operand flops. The DSP reads the ID/EX
rs1_val/rs2_val flops that already exist. They also drive the ALU
adder, comparator, AGU and bypass mux, so they cannot be absorbed.
CoreMark's MUL operands come almost only from LH/LW. The load-use
interlock already puts the MUL in ID while the load sits in MEM, so ID
resolves those operands through mem_fwd_val and a MUL almost never needs
the EX/MEM -> EX bypass. The bypass is paying Fmax on every cycle for a
case that is close to free to handle another way.

or new operand flops that Gowin absorbed into the DSP input registers.
r9s0's lesson named that absorption as the cause: dedicated flops that
feed only the DSP get pulled into its fixed-column input register.
This plan adds no new operand flops. The DSP reads the ID/EX
rs1_val/rs2_val flops that already exist. They also drive the ALU
adder, comparator, AGU and bypass mux, so they cannot be absorbed.
CoreMark's MUL operands come almost only from LH/LW. The load-use
interlock already puts the MUL in ID while the load sits in MEM, so ID
resolves those operands through mem_fwd_val and a MUL almost never needs
the EX/MEM -> EX bypass. The bypass is paying Fmax on every cycle for a
case that is close to free to handle another way.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
(A) The core change, 0 new flops and 0 new stall/flush sources.
1. alu.sv: add two ports, mul_a_in and mul_b_in, fed from the bare
   ID/EX flops (in.rs1_val, in.rs2_val). For MUL* alu_src = 0, so
   rs2_val == op_b. The DSP operands, the sign-extension bits (a_signed,
   b_signed, which are already registered) and the ALTOPS mul_lo/mul_hi
   stand-ins all use mul_a_in/mul_b_in in place of the bypassed a/b.
   A MUL that retires never needed the bypass (see 2), so for every
   retired MUL the bare and bypassed operands are equal. That keeps the
   real and ALTOPS branches consistent and keeps rvfi rs1/rs2_rdata
   right: they still come from the bypassed rs1/rs2 in ex_stage.
   Leave the fast_or / mul_or syn_keep split and the final
   out = fast_or | mul_or exactly as they are. Only the DSP's input
   source changes.
2. id_stage.sv: a conservative, EX-independent MUL-bypass detector on
   the raw instruction and the ID/EX flops only:
     mul_fix = dec_is_mul && reg_q.ctrl.reg_write && reg_q.rd != 0 &&
               (reg_q.rd == rs1 || reg_q.rd == rs2)
   where dec_is_mul = alu_sel[RS_MULLO] | alu_sel[RS_MULHI].
   ex_wb_kill is left out on purpose. Replaying when the producer's
   write was killed anyway is correct, only slower, and it keeps the
   EX redirect cone out of this term. Fold mul_fix into the existing
   replay machinery, which r9s2 already uses for bad BTB predictions:
     replay = (bad_pt && (br_okd || dec_is_jalr)) || mul_fix
     early  = (jal_okd && !in.pt) || bad_pt || mul_fix
   e_tgt already selects in.pc under replay, reg_write is already
   cleared by replay in ID, and EX already drops valid under replay.
   So the redirect cone, flush_id and the EX/MEM D inputs get no new
   term. early and replay stay single registered bits, so EX logic is
   input-for-input the same as r9s2. Liveness: the refetched MUL
   reaches ID one cycle after its replay redirect. By then the ID/EX
   occupant is a flushed bubble (reg_write = 0), so mul_fix cannot
   fire twice and the producer is covered by the MEM forward or the
   regfile write-first path.
   BTB training stays correct: t_clr = valid && pt && !jfix &&
   !(br_ok && !replay). A MUL fetched with pt=1 already takes the
   bad_pt path, and a MUL never has br_ok. Make sure a replayed MUL
   with pt=0 does not trigger t_clr (valid && pt is 0) and does not
   count as a branch (t_br needs br_ok).
Cost in cycles: about 3 per replayed MUL (redirect bubble plus refetch,
~22% imem stall), and only for a MUL whose operand comes from the
instruction just before it. In the -O3 CoreMark matrix kernels the
producer is an LH that load-use already separates. The implementer
must measure the cosim cycle count against r9s2's 4,215,892 and report
how many replays happen. Expect under 0.3%.
Why this removes a real level: the DSP input net is now a plain flop
Q, not flop -> 2:1 LUT -> 32 fanout-2 routes. That removes one LUT4
and one general-routing hop (about 1.2-1.8 ns on GW2A) from the
deepest family. It also takes 66 DSP input loads off the alu_result
and fwd*_ex nets. Those nets are the start of the adder loop, the
redirect cone and the load/ID forward, so the other tied families get
lighter too and lose routing delay, not just placement luck.
(B) Build only if the option-1 report after A shows the adder/shifter
loop on top: nothing else. Do NOT touch the IF pc_w loop, the result
OR join after the DSP, or the load-forward mux. The lessons show each
of those changes has regressed alone.
Required verification, reported in implementation_notes:
- the Gowin netlist shows the multiplier's input registers unused
  (combinational DSP, AREG/BREG off) and rs1_val/rs2_val still in
  fabric;
- option-1 top-10 paths with and without A, and where the DSP loop
  ranks;
- the cosim cycle count and the number of MUL replays.

title: Fetch-side 64-word L0 instruction store that hides imem-not-ready cycles (look-ahead, flop-registered)
motivation:
After the BTB, the largest remaining loss in r9s2 is imem-not-ready: the
stall generator refuses ~22% of cycles, so every fetch costs 1/0.78 =
1.28 cycles, about 0.28 CPI of r9s2's ~1.444 CPI (4,215,892 cycles /
2.92M instructions). That is roughly 20% of all cycles, more than the
redirect, dmem and load-use losses combined. Every change tried against it
so far (the r5s1/r10s1 IQs) only overlapped imem stalls with back-end
stalls, which are too rare, and got 1.5%. Nothing has changed where
instructions come from. The harness only times the core, so a
structure that supplies an already-fetched word when the bus says
not-ready removes the stall itself. CoreMark's timed region spends most of
its instructions in short inner loops (crc, list_find, matrix inner
products, the state-machine scan loop). Also, ten r9s2 derivatives
(r10s0-r14s2) show that Fmax-only edits on this base land at ~102 MHz,
below the scored 106.1. To clear the 4.6% bar, a change needs a large cycle
cut whose added logic stays off the tied EX / redirect / load-forward
families.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a small direct-mapped instruction store to if_stage, 64 entries of one
word each, indexed by word PC bits [7:2]. It is built as a look-ahead in the
same way as the proven r9s2 BTB, so every signal it adds to the fetch/ID
datapath is a flop.

(1) Storage. LUT-RAM (syn_ramstyle distributed_ram). Each entry holds
    {valid, tag = pc[19:8] (12 bits), instr[31:2] (30 bits)}, 43 bits in
    11 RAM16 columns x 4 rows. instr[1:0] is always 2'b11 for a cacheable
    word. A fetched word with [1:0] != 2'b11 is written with valid = 0, so
    it always comes from imem. Twelve tag bits cover the full legal 1 MB
    code space exactly, so there is no aliasing and no partial tag. That
    matters because, unlike the BTB, a wrong hit here is not re-checked.
    Fill uses flops only: on every cycle with io_imemReady = 1, write
    {1, pc_w[19:8], io_imemData[31:2]} at pc_w[7:2]. That is one sync
    write port (addr = pc_w flops, data = the imem word, WE = imem_ready
    flop). Verilator gets an `initial` zero fill, like btb_mem. The FPGA
    LUT-RAM powers up to 0, so valid = 0. Formal is unaffected by arbitrary
    initial content, because the wrapper's imem word is already symbolic.
(2) Look-ahead read. Read asynchronously at npc_seq[5:0], the same kept
    net and index that the BTB lookup already uses. Register the raw
    {valid, tag, instr} into cq_* flops under CE = !stall, exactly like
    pt_q/hit_q/tgt18_q, with no redirect term. The tag compare is NOT done
    on the npc_seq path. The npc_seq path therefore gets only a
    RAM16 -> 2 MUX2 levels -> D leg, no deeper than the BTB's
    RAM16 -> 8-bit compare -> D. redir_q already means "the look-ahead
    flops do not describe pc_w", so it also masks the cache.
(3) Hit and stall. In the fetch cycle,
    c_hit = cq_valid & (cq_tag == pc_w[19:8]) & ~redir_q. This is 3 LUT4
    levels from flops only. Export c_hit to core.sv. hazard_unit's
    imem_stall becomes !imem_ready & !c_hit, so stall_if, flush_id and
    the PC/BTB CE see one more flop-sourced term, well short of the
    11-level redirect cone. The fetch word to ID is
    instr = imem_ready ? io_imemData : {cq_instr, 2'b11}, one LUT level
    with a flop select (imem_ready comes from bench_stall_gen flops).
    if_id.instr, the raw rs1/rs2 fields fed to hazard_unit, and ID's
    regfile addresses and forward compares all read this muxed word
    instead of io_imemData. Everything downstream (the kill-bit flush,
    BTB pred_off/replay, the forward selects) is unchanged, because a hit
    delivers exactly the architectural word at pc_w.
(4) Liveness and correctness. The first fetch after any redirect has
    redir_q = 1 and always waits for the bus, so replays still make
    progress. A hit returns the word fetched from the same full word
    address, so no replay/kill path is needed. Nothing is added to EX,
    MEM, the redirect cone or the ID/EX kill bits.

Expected cycles: with hit fraction H of non-post-redirect fetches, the
saving is ~0.28*H CPI. The implementer MUST measure H before synthesis
with a trace model or cosim cycle count; 64 entries should catch the
inner loops, and H ~0.6-0.8 gives -12% to -16% cycles. If cosim shows the
cut below ~9%, try 32 entries (half the RAM16s) and 128 entries and keep
the best cycles-vs-area point, following r9s2's rule to size at the knee.
Fmax budget: the only new logic on existing families is one mux LUT on
the fetch word before ID decode and the regfile LUT-RAM address, plus ~44
RAM16s, ~60 FFs and ~60 LUTs of area. Expect the median to land in
r9s2's derivative band (~100-104 MHz). At ~3.65M cycles and 101 MHz,
fitness is ~277 (+10%). At 97 MHz it is still ~266 (+5.6%).

lesson: - 2026-09-30 hyp-20260930-002-r15s1 (regression, -0.44%): A 64-entry look-ahead L0 instruction store (LUT-RAM filled on every imem_ready cycle, read at npc_seq into cq_* flops, c_hit = flop compare & ~redir_q, imem_stall = !imem_ready & !c_hit, ID word = imem_ready ? io_imemData : {cq_instr, 2'b11}) produced the largest measured cycle cut on r9s2 so far, 4,215,892 -> 3,646,109 (-13.5%; 32/128/256 entries gave -12.2/-15.7/-17.7%, with no knee), but the evaluated Fmax fell from 106.1 to 91.4 MHz (LUT4 2681 -> 3101, not the planned ~60 LUTs), just under the 91.8 MHz break-even; since 64 and 128 entries timed alike (~88 MHz at place option 0), the loss comes from the "one LUT" fetch-word mux, not the storage: it sits in front of ID decode, the regfile LUT-RAM address and the forward compares, and it put the load-use compare back on a muxed word instead of r2s0's raw io_imemData (the implementer's timing listed bus-ready -> fetch-word mux -> decode among the worst paths), so a retry must keep raw io_imemData on those ID/hazard consumers (e.g. give the L0 word its own path into ID) and size by cycles-vs-Fmax, because 256 entries at the same 91.4 MHz would already score about 263.

title: Predicted-path fetch hold: a 1-entry word latch that keeps the BTB-steered fetch that arrived during a back-end stall, so the refetch cannot miss the imem bus
motivation:
The branch predictor has run out of direction and target work. The
calibrated trace model leaves about 82K redirect bubbles (1.9% of r9s2's
4,215,892 cycles): 17K capacity misses, 13.7K JALR returns, 6.6K taken
transfers right after a redirect, and the rest are data-dependent direction
mispredicts. A perfect direction and target predictor would still cut less
than 2% of cycles, which is under the 4.6% bar. Every Fmax-only predictor
edit on r9s2 has landed at 96.5-105.1 MHz (r10s2, r11s2, r12s2, r13s2,
r14s2).
The prediction the BTB makes is still wasted in one place. When a back-end
stall holds the PC (load-use, dmem stall, DIV), the word fetched along the
predicted path in that cycle is thrown away, and the same address is fetched
again. The refetch then misses the free-running xorshift bus 22% of the time
(expected +0.28 cycles each). r9s2 has about 0.2M load-use bubbles and about
0.2M dmem-stall cycles. The BTB + 2-entry IQ composite measured 4,011,459
cycles (-4.9% vs r9s2), so this waste is real. That composite lost 8-18 MHz
to the queue's mux in front of decode, the 134 banked flops, and the IQ
terms on flush_id (r8s1, r9s1, r10s1).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add one 32-bit hold latch plus a valid flop, and nothing else: no queue, no
occupancy counter, no second pred_off bank, and no new term on redirect or
on the EX cones.
  hold_q    <= io_imemData    when (stall_if && io_imemReady && !redirect && !hold_v_q)
  hold_v_q  <= 1              on that same capture
            <= 0              when the PC advances or redirect fires
While hold_v_q is set, if_stage treats the fetch as ready (fetch_ok =
io_imemReady | hold_v_q). So the stall_if/flush_id imem term becomes
!fetch_ok, and ID reads the held word through a 2:1 mux whose select is a
single flop.
The prediction state needs no change. cur_q (pt/hit/ctr/tgt18) already
holds under stall, and pc_w does not move while hold_v_q is set, so
pred_off and the look-ahead lookup describe the held word exactly. A
redirect clears hold_v_q, and the held word is never used on a new path.
To keep the mux off the tied families:
(1) Feed the regfile read addresses, the load-use compare and the
    fwd*_mem compares from a kept 10-bit field mux (rs1/rs2 bits only):
    one LUT3 with a flop select ahead of the LUTRAM address.
(2) Give decoder/imm_gen/pred_off their own copy of the full-word mux, so
    synthesis does not merge it with (1).
(3) Leave redirect, flush_id's redirect term, and the ID/EX kill bits
    unchanged. hold_v_q enters only the imem-stall leg of flush_id and
    stall_if, where io_imemReady already sits.
Expected cycles come from the same xorshift model the IQ used. A 1-entry
non-bypassing hold recovers the refetch miss after every back-end stall
that saw a ready bus: about 0.22 x (load-use + dmem + DIV stall events) =
about 70-100K cycles. That is -1.7% to -2.4%, or about half of the 2-entry
IQ's -4.9%. It costs about 45 LUT/FF, against the IQ's roughly 250.
Implementation must measure cycles in cosim first (with --istall and
dstall), and report option-1 timing for the ID/EX D side
(imem -> hold mux -> LUTRAM -> rs*_res) before scoring.

lesson: - 2026-09-30 hyp-20260930-003-r15s2 (regression, -6.20%): A 1-entry fetch hold (hold_q/hold_v_q, ~45 planned LUT/FF, a flop-selected 2:1 mux in front of ID split into a syn_keep'd 10-bit rs-field copy for the regfile LUT-RAM address, load-use and fwd*_mem compares plus a kept full-word copy for decode, and fetch_ok = imem_ready | hold_v_q on stall_if/flush_id) scored 236.14, an implied median (10*Fmax/Mcycles) of ~97-100 MHz anywhere between r9s2's 4,215,892 cycles and the planned -2.4% (the required cosim count and option-1 timing were not reported), in the lower part of the 96.5-105.1 MHz range of r9s2 derivatives and far below the ~111 MHz the bar needs; together with r15s1 (91.4 MHz with a bus-ready select and +420 LUTs), this suggests that a second source for the ID word costs Fmax even with a flop select, few LUTs and split kept copies, because the mux sits on the data leg as an extra LUT level between the imem BSRAM output and the regfile LUT-RAM address and ID compares (r13s1's BSRAM-sourced ID/EX D family), and neither select timing nor copy placement can remove that level; so on r9s2, which has no IF/ID register, count any fetch-word mux as a lost level on that family, and pursue a fetch-side cycle cut only if its cosim-measured size clears the 4.6% bar plus several MHz of Fmax loss (as the L0 store's -13.5% to -17.7% might), never for a small refetch saving like this plan's own -1.7% to -2.4% estimate, which fell short of the bar even at zero Fmax cost.
